entries.title: Brookfield Zoo welcomes newborn squirrel monkey
entries.summary: <p>Amid the humid mist and roaring waterfalls inside Brookfield Zoo’s Tropic World habitat, a new, tiny resident clung tightly to its mother and made an exclusive Sun-Times debut.</p><p>A newborn squirrel monkey born July 30 to mother Gizmo and father Sandy. While the infant does not have a name yet and its sex remains unidentified, it is already thriving, spending its first days riding securely on its mother’s chest and back as she navigates the habitat.</p><p>Guests will have a chance to see the newborn squirrel monkey and the rest of the primates inside the Tropic World exhibit daily during regular park hours.</p><p>The birth marks a milestone for the monkey troop and for Kim Skelton, director of primate care and conservation at Brookfield Zoo Chicago. Skelton brings 25 years of primate care experience from the Denver Zoo to the Brookfield team.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/10/31/18338371/2-baby-squirrel-monkeys-born-at-brookfield-zoo" target="_blank" >“Gizmo has had lots of babies</a> before,” said Skelton, but “this is Sandy, the father's, first infant. Him and Gizmo created this perfect little infant that's pretty adorable.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel Enhancement" active group of six squirrel monkeys, including aunts and older sibling Slim, who was born in a previous litter and is currently learning maternal behaviors by watching Gizmo. Skelton said that mother primates tend to serve as living models for their other offspring when it comes to motherhood. Allowing young females like Slim to observe daily interactions and practice key maternal behavior.</p><p>The troop of monkeys share their habitat with other animals, including capuchins, spider monkeys, and a giant anteater. The troop manages its own social structure smoothly, with Skelton noting that squirrel monkeys naturally stick to the mid-level branches while anteaters remain on the ground. The group also occasionally interacts with<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/metro-state/2025/02/18/brookfield-zoo-endangered-spider-monkeys-rescued-wildlife-trafficking" target="_blank" > neighboring spider monkeys</a>.</p><p>For now, the newborn will remain dependent on mom.</p><p>“That’s at least a few months before they start experimenting and getting off mom,” Skelton said. “It’ll be a while before they actually go off and explore on their own.”</p><p>As the infant grows, the primate care specialists will track key milestones, watching as the infant starts eating solid foods and engaging in social interactions without its mother nearby.</p><p>Another key milestone the Brookfield team will look for is when the infant starts using its long tail for balance. Unlike many South American primates with prehensile tails used for grasping, a squirrel monkey’s tail is longer than its body and functions more like a cat’s tail to help as they leap through trees.</p><p>“All of our births, whether it's a squirrel monkey, a gorilla, or a giraffe feed into our Species Survival Programs or captive management breeding programs that support not just populations within zoos, but potentially wild populations as well,” Skelton said.</p><p>That Species Survival Programs is managed through the Association of Zoos and Aquariums. These breeding initiatives maintain genetically diverse populations across accredited institutions, tracking lineages to safeguard species and support potential wild reintroductions.</p><p>“Every birth matters," Skelton said, "and we’re just pumped to have another little one popping around.”</p>

entries.title: Rubber duck race helps Special Olympics pay the bills
entries.summary: <p>More than 90,000 rubber ducks raced/floated/bobbed haphazardly toward the finish line near the Columbus Drive Bridge Thursday morning as thousands of spectators lined the Riverwalk to cheer them on.</p><p>It was all part of what has become an annual tradition to raise money for Special Olympics Illinois.</p><p>Since 2005, the Chicago Ducky Derby has invited people to adopt rubber ducks starting at $10 each, with bigger sponsor packs available. The ducks are dumped into the Chicago River and head toward the finish line. The money raised helps provide year-round sports programming, adaptive equipment and other resources for athletes with intellectual disabilities.</p><p>By noon, the riverfront near the Columbus Drive Bridge was packed with spectators holding up their phones, waiting for the dump truck to release more than 90,000 yellow rubber duckies into the water.</p><p>This year's event raised more than $700,000 for Special Olympics Illinois. The sponsor of the first-place duck won a new Chevrolet Trax. The second-place duck's sponsor won $2,500 in cash, and third place got four club seats to a Chicago Cubs game.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: 57 decomposing bodies discovered at Far South Side funeral home
entries.summary: <p>Dozens of decomposing bodies were found Thursday at a Far South Side funeral home, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office.</p><p>A funeral was in progress when police, acting on a tip, showed up at South Chicago Chapel, 2939 E. 95th St., police said. Police had been told bodies at the home were not being stored at or below 40 degrees, as required by state regulations, according to a police report obtained by the Sun-Times.</p><p>Officers were met by funeral director Clark Morgan, who accompanied them on a walk-through of the building. During the walk-through, they found 57 bodies in various areas of the funeral home. The bodies were not refrigerated, and were in various states of decomposition, according to the police report.</p><p>At some point, officers left the building, and when they tried to go back inside. Morgan told officers that on the advice of his attorney, he wasn't letting them back in without a warrant. After officers told Morgan they did not need a warrant to inspect the building during operating hours, he padlocked the door and left, according to the report. Officers then called the Chicago Fire Department to help gain entry to the building.</p><p>The business’ license was revoked Wednesday, according to the police report.</p><p>The area around the home was blocked off by police Thursday night as some neighbors continued to mill about. </p><p>The foul smell that hung in the air Thursday night started during the winter, several neighbors told the Sun-Times.</p><p>One pair of neighbors were initially thrown off by the late hours people would be working at the funeral home. One, who worked night shift, said he’d often see in the lot past midnight.</p><p>They said they ended up putting up traps for the thousands of flies that emanated from the building. They, along with other neighbors, reported it to law enforcement six months ago, they said.</p><p>“We're grateful,” one neighbor said of the investigation. “I thought it was weird. … [But] we had an idea of what was going on.”</p><p>In a statement, the medical examiner’s office said it had been notified by Illinois and Chicago officials of the improperly stored bodies. Investigators and forensic pathologists went to the funeral home on Thursday and found "more than 50 decedents in various states of decomposition."</p><p>Staff from the medical examiner's office are "assessing the conditions of the remains, searching for documentation regarding identification of the decedents as well as death certificates. This process could take several days to ensure proper disposition," according to the statement. The office "will work with authorities to identify these decedents as quickly as possible and notify their families."</p><p>Another neighbor said whenever people would enter or exit the building for a funeral, “you could smell the rot.”</p><p>“We thought at first it was coming from a factory nearby, but it was like a rotting smell,” another neighbor said. “It smelled like an animal that was dead. … It wasn’t once or twice, it was every weekend. It was a fight to go outside and get in the car.”</p><p>“We just hope the families find their loved ones,” she added.</p><p>The Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation suspended the license of the registered funeral director Johanna Morgan. Her husband previously held a a funeral director and embalmer intern license, which was revoked in 2024, according to the department.</p><p>That department alerted authorities after investigating.</p><p>A message left on the voicemail inbox of the funeral home Thursday was not returned.</p><p>A one-star Google review of the chapel posted two weeks ago complained: "HORRIBLE!! It smells and they are very unprofessional."</p><p><i>Contributing: Rosemary Sobol, Lauren FitzPatrick</i><br></p>

entries.title: Playoff expansion is No. 1 storyline ahead of the high school football season
entries.summary: <p>Is it time for a new catchphrase in prep football?</p><p>For decades, coaches have talked about the “drive for five,” which refers to the number of victories generally needed to clinch an IHSA playoff berth.</p><p>But this fall, that number will change for the first time in 25 years.</p><p>That’s the biggest storyline heading into the 2026 season. Here’s a rundown of a few to watch:</p><p><b>Expanded playoffs</b></p><p>For the first time since the IHSA went from six to eight classes in 2001, the postseason field is getting bigger.</p><p>After years of debate and various proposals, IHSA member schools voted to expand the playoffs by 50% from 256 to 384 teams.</p><p>That change has led to a few more, including the earliest start to football practice in state history on Wednesday. This year’s regular season starts on Aug. 20 in order to accommodate an extra playoff round and still finish the postseason over Thanksgiving weekend.</p><p>The new format introduces byes for the first time in the football playoffs’ 52-year history. Two-thirds of the teams will play in the opening round over the weekend of Oct. 23-24, with the winners advancing to the first round against bye teams Oct. 30-31.</p><p>Playoff guru Steve Soucie of Friday Night Drive has projected that all three-win teams will earn playoff berths along with two-win teams with a good strength of schedule.</p><p>The bar to reach the postseason has been lowered. But many coaches are still aiming for five wins or more in hopes of getting home-field advantage in the opening round or earning a bye.</p><p><b>Conference realignment</b></p><p>There are some new league alignments for 2026, though the pace of change has slowed from its peak.</p><p>After operating as a football-only superconference the last two years, the nine-team SouthWest Suburban and six-team DuPage Valley have gone their separate ways. Though the split has led to some scheduling challenges with nonconference games later in the season, it has allowed the restoration of rivalries that were paused during the merger.</p><p>The 24-team Catholic League is no longer co-branded with the East Suburban Catholic Conference, which disbanded at the end of the last school year.</p><p>There was shuffling throughout the league’s six divisions. Some of the highlights included Marist replacing St. Ignatius in the top-level Catholic Blue and defending Class 4A champion Montini moving to the Green to join reigning 5A champ St. Francis, 7A runner-up St. Rita and 6A semifinalist Nazareth.</p><p>The Public League also has a new look. In place of the former top-level Red Metro, which had 16 teams, are two top-tier, six-team divisions: the Red Star and Red Shield. What was formerly the top White tier is now the second-tier Red. The new White and the Blue round out the Public League tiers.</p><p><b>Holecek’s back</b></p><p>The biggest coaching change comes at Loyola, where John Holecek is back in charge after a three-year hiatus.</p><p>In his first stint from 2006 to 2022, Holecek turned a solidly successful program into arguably the state’s best. His teams went 185-36 with three state titles and four runner-up finishes.</p><p>He was succeeded by Beau Desherow, who led the Ramblers to state titles in 2023 and 2024. Loyola went 4-5 last season, its first losing record since 2002.</p><p>Holecek returned to the staff as an assistant and now begins his second act. Desherow has shifted to a newly created position of general manager of the football program as well as assistant head coach.<br></p>

entries.title: Sueños DJ, husband detained by immigration agents at Midway Airport despite pending asylum case
entries.summary: <p>Omar David Panqueva and his husband Santiago Paez had been set to depart on a flight to Washington D.C. to start a series of Karol G afterparties following her tour around the country Sunday.</p><p>Panqueva, known as DJ TUNJO, performed at Sueños Music Festival in Grant Park in May and the couple founded the Chicago-based Latin music and community event organization La Mesa Presents.</p><p>As they exited an Uber to go into Midway Airport, they were surrounded and detained by federal agents.</p><p>Silvia Paez, Santiago’s sister, described the two in social media posts as “not only partners, but a power team.” She said in a statement that the couple had been taken to a detention center in Indiana after being detained at Midway.</p><p>“They are good within the circumstances,” she wrote on social media. “[But] they are still separated.”</p><p>The Department of Homeland Security said it detained the couple for overstaying their 2021 visas that expired in 2022, but wouldn’t say if the two were accused of any crimes or had pending asylum cases the department was aware of.</p><p>Both will be held “pending removal hearings,” the federal agency said.</p><p>However, their attorney, Enrique Espinoza, said the two had pending asylum cases, and that those cases had been filed within the legally mandated time after their arrival in the United States, but the government was “skipping past that part.”</p><p>He said the couple had been cooperating with the government on the pending case, even providing the required biometric information.</p><p>“They have been proactive [in] requesting information about the status of their case, and the government said they were working on it,” Espinoza told the Sun-Times. “And here we are now with them detained even though they followed every rule by the government and have no criminal background. … It seems like they were just easy targets.”</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/help-us-free-santiago-and-david-dj-tunjo" target="_blank" ><u>GoFundMe</u></a> for the couple’s legal defense and travel costs had raised $21,000 by Thursday evening. The couple’s lawyer didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Paez’s sister urged people to “be safe” and avoid airports. She also wrote that the support and “how much people are caring” was “one of the things keeping them strong.”</p><p>“Santiago and David are very aware of how the community has shown up for them,” Paez’s sister said. “They are so grateful for all of your support and your kindness, and overwhelmed by the love coming from you guys.”</p><p>In another social media, she said: "I wish we lived in a world where being Latino wasn’t a crime."</p>

entries.title: White Sox let five leads get away in brutal 13-inning loss to red-hot Red Sox
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON — When it was finally over, the press-box announcer read the time of the game, 4 hours, 23 minutes — “like the old days.”</p><p>He was referring to the Red Sox’ old days, particularly in their rivalry with the Yankees, before the advent of the pitch clock. But for the White Sox, the old days are the last three seasons, each of which ended with more than 100 losses.</p><p>While the Red Sox refused to lose, the White Sox refused to win, blowing five leads and falling 12-11 in 13 often agonizing innings. The Red Sox swept the three-game series and the season series, extended their winning streak to eight and improved to 31-5 since June 25.</p><p>“Good battle there,” White Sox manager Will Venable said. “Some things that we could control, you wish you had back. But gotta give the Red Sox credit. The hardest team to beat right now. We’ve seen it firsthand. The record against them speaks for itself.”</p><p>The White Sox led 7-6 in the bottom of the ninth with newly acquired reliever Huascar Brazoban one strike from leaving the tying run on third. But Wilyer Abreu singled to center, and the wackiness began.</p><p>After the White Sox scored twice in the 10th on Chase Meidroth’s second two-run homer of the game into the Monster seats, the Red Sox tied it. After the White Sox scored once in the 11th and 12th, the Red Sox tied it. And after the White Sox left a runner on third in the 13th, the outcome felt inevitable.</p><p>Sure enough, Erick Fedde, who pitched three innings two days ago, allowed Caleb Durbin’s winning single.</p><p>Lost in the madness was newly acquired Luis Castillo, who gave the White Sox exactly what they had hoped for in his first start — for two innings. After retiring the first seven batters he faced and being staked to a 4-0 lead, Castillo walked No. 8 hitter Anthony Seigler and allowed a home run to No. 9 Connor Wong, only his third of the season.</p><p>After the White Sox added a run in the top of the fourth, Castillo’s wheels came off in the bottom half, when he allowed two singles and two doubles that led to three runs. He left after four innings, allowing five runs, six hits and one walk with five strikeouts.</p><p>“The fastball command, the walk ahead of the Wong home run,” Venable said of Castillo’s issue. “And then it just kind of piled up on him; couldn’t put guys away.”</p><p>Making matters worse, the White Sox lost newly acquired catcher Joey Bart to a fractured left hand when he was hit by a pitch. He’ll go on the injured list.</p><p>“It’s a tough series, no doubt about it, especially with a chance to win tonight and end things on a good note here on a tough road trip,” Venable said. “I think there’s a bunch of stuff that obviously we got to do a better job of.”</p><h3>Venable mixing it up</h3><p>Venable said he’s going to start using the designated-hitter spot to give Munetaka Murakami, Miguel Vargas and Colson Montgomery opportunities against left-handed pitchers. Part of that strategy will be tapping into Luisangel Acuna’s versatility. Venable gave Acuna his first start of the season in left field Thursday, forcing him to contend with the Green Monster.</p><p>“Obviously, Fenway is unique,” Venable said before the game. “I thought it was actually a good spot to expose him to for the first time. He’ll run down some flyballs today, get a feel for it. And really the way you approach the wall is pretty simple. Everything off the wall, you just fire into second base.”</p><p>The ball found Acuna quickly. Red Sox leadoff man Nick Sogard flew out to him. But Acuna’s stay was short. After the Red Sox replaced left-handed starter Ranger Suarez with righty Greg Weissert in the fourth, left-handed-hitting and regular left fielder Sam Antonacci took over.</p><p>Venable also said he might’ve undervalued Randal Grichuk’s defense and will look to play him in left field more, as well. Venable largely has been platooning the right-handed-hitting Grichuk and the left-handed-hitting Andrew Benintendi at DH.</p><p>“I just think we need to be flexible in some ways, especially for those big guys that are out there every day,” Venable said. “Maybe instead of an off day, we can keep their bat in the lineup.”</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>Double-A Birmingham outfielder James Taussig and High-A Winston-Salem right-handed pitcher Jake Curtis were named the Sox’ minor-league player and pitcher of the month for July. Curtis is a native of Downstate Chatham and has known Springfield-native Antonacci since they were children.</p><p>• Shortstop Roch Cholowsky, whom the Sox took with the first pick in the draft last month, hit his first professional home run Thursday, an opposite-field three-run shot in his third game for Winston-Salem.</p><p>• Bulls TV voice Adam Amin, former White Sox catcher A.J. Pierzynski, Adam Wainwright and Ken Rosenthal will call the Sox’ game against the Guardians at 6:15 p.m. Saturday on Fox 32.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: El-Sayed has his work cut out between now and November
entries.summary: <p>Far-left progressive Abdul El-Sayed is the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, a swing state that Donald Trump won twice.</p><p>It was the first major test of an ascendant progressive wing of the Democratic Party looking to see how far they could push their agenda outside of liberal strongholds like New York City — and he passed it. But just barely, and the warning signs on the horizon are flashing red.</p><p>See, El-Sayed defeated moderate Rep. Haley Stevens by just a percentage point — winning 48.5% of the vote to her 47.5% — thereby winning a plurality of the Democratic vote, not a majority.</p><p>That means he’s got some work to do between now and November.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b70000" name="module-b70000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>He’s, as my colleague and Michigan native Jamal Simmons put it, a very talented “political athlete,” but Michigan Democrats — like all Democrats, it seems — are deeply divided on which direction to take the country and which messages will work best to win big in November. And you better believe the general election will expose all the ugly and treacherous fault lines.</p><p>While the issue of Israel has been front and center — intentionally put there by many progressives who believe it a defining one, for better or worse — there are other divides in the party that candidates like El-Sayed will have to reckon with, and quickly.</p><p>One of the major schisms on the left right now is between progressives and Black voters, many of whom, especially older Black voters, aren’t supportive of the socialist agenda these candidates are openly pushing and prefer, instead of moderate candidates who are focused on kitchen-table issues.</p><p>To wit, Stevens was <a class="Link" href="https://www.foxnews.com/politics/swing-state-poll-spells-trouble-far-left-schumer-backed-candidate-dominates-critical-voting-blocs" target="_blank" >leading among</a> Black voters in Michigan by a whopping 46 points before the primary, and she <a class="Link" href="https://bridgemi.com/michigan-government/how-abdul-el-sayed-won-michigan-big-turnout-liberal-towns-walkup-votes/" target="_blank" >delivered them</a> on Tuesday night.</p><p>Of the 12 Michigan counties with large Black voter populations, El-Sayed won just five, and Stevens won seven. He also lost all of metro Detroit, the state’s largest Black-majority city, where Stevens won handily, with 60%.</p><p>El-Sayed and another far-left progressive candidate — William Lawrence, who also won his primary in Michigan’s 7th District — have earned the ire of Black leadership, with revered party elder Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., <a class="Link" href="https://www.mediaite.com/politics/james-clyburn-rips-el-sayeds-rallies-for-lack-of-diversity-tells-me-all-i-need-to-know/" target="_blank" >scolding</a> the former for not having more Black support at his rallies. Likewise, a PAC for the Congressional Black Caucus also released <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/5964228-progressive-house-candidate-responds-to-criticism-over-past-comments-about-black-dems/" target="_blank" >a statement</a> telling their supporters not to vote for Lawrence over comments he made about Israel and Black leadership.</p><p>So, suffice it to say, El-Sayed will have to do what other progressives like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., could not — bring Black voters out to cast their ballots for him.</p><p>The questions, if not the answers, are clear. With Stevens out, will moderate Black voters simply stay home? Could they possibly vote for Republican Mike Rogers, who lost to moderate Dem Elissa Slotkin in 2024 by less than 0.3%?</p><p>Will Black leaders like Clyburn change their tune about El-Sayed now that he’s officially the nominee? If New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s race was any indication, the answer is no — Clyburn endorsed his rival, the more moderate Andrew Cuomo, in that election.</p><p>Can El-Sayed and others, who had to run far to the left to engage their base in a primary, make an effective pivot to the center in time for November? Will they risk alienating their supporters if they do?</p><p>It’s a tricky road ahead for an energized and emboldened group of candidates who are about to test out messages and agendas to a much wider audience and fend off all the scrutiny that comes with that.</p><p>Either El-Sayed will prove this new wave of progressives could be key to turning swing states blue, retaking the majority and reinvigorating a lackluster Democratic Party, or Dems will be wishing, come November, that they stuck with the safer choice.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-870000" name="module-870000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Educators, play your trading cards right in classrooms, extracurricular activities
entries.summary: <p>Trading cards have shaped popular culture for over a century, and their appeal remains strong even as digital activities dominate our lives.</p><p>As education evolves, trading cards stand out as tools that bridge analog play with the cognitive demands of the digital age.</p><p>The hobby naturally develops executive function by helping kids plan, organize and manage resources. It also creates organic opportunities to practice math and reading comprehension.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-400000" name="module-400000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>According to <a class="Link" href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7038459" target="_blank" >recent research</a>, not only do trading cards tap into reward systems like those found in digital experiences — intermittent reinforcement and variable outcomes — they also improve learning outcomes.</p><p>This is especially vital now, as school systems adapt to students who are raised constantly in front of screens. We have seen how digital oversaturation affects learning: shortened attention spans, information fatigue, lower tolerance for complex tasks and increased demand for instant gratification.</p><p>Trading card-related educational activities can undo some of those harms as they incentivizes patience, critical thinking and collaboration with peers.</p><p>Analysis shows that trading cards serve as valuable learning artifacts that support the skills necessary to thrive in STEAM — science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics — classrooms. When integrated within digital learning environments, trading cards can enhance academic outcomes by supporting literacy and content understanding, cognitive and conceptual processing and even <a class="Link" href="https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257198765_Multimodality_A_Social_Semiotic_Approach_to_Contemporary_Communication_Gunther_Kress_Routledge_London_2010_212_pp_45_bw_illustrations_15_colour_plates_ISBN_13_978-0-415-32061-0_pbk" target="_blank" >multimodal reasoning</a>, a type of cross-format thinking that allows students to make sense of information coming from different sources at once.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://doingsocialstudies.com/2014/03/24/trading-cards-readwritethink-and-the-common-core/" target="_blank" >Trading cards</a> help to put critical thinking and problem-solving into practice. So not only are students engaging with <a class="Link" href="https://www.researchgate.net/publication/262326293_Collection_creation_and_community_a_discussion_on_collectible_card_games" target="_blank" >compelling card templates</a> that help them synthesize complex information, but they're also simultaneously revealing the relationships within complex systems.</p><p>Card collecting’s appeal among young students can be used as an effective tool outside the classroom as well, in summer programs, to help kids learn executive functioning skills and return in the fall well prepared to tackle their curriculum.</p><p>Such programs have already been implemented this year through after-school programs and clubs.</p><p>At McDonough Middle School in Hartford, Connecticut, a volunteer leads a weekly <a class="Link" href="https://www.ccaoh.org/pokemon-cards-help-students-learn-about-business/" target="_blank" >after-school session</a> in which students learn to assess card values, understand market dynamics and think like young entrepreneurs.</p><p>Kenowa Hills Middle School in Michigan reports that card-focused clubs have grown from a handful of students to nearly 50 participants, with school officials saying they have seen <a class="Link" href="https://www.schoolnewsnetwork.org/2023/04/21/card-club-plays-it-forward/" target="_blank" >measurable gains</a> in social skill-building among students.</p><p>Using <a class="Link" href="https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/8/1030" target="_blank" >card-based games</a> as a serious learning medium isn't a new concept. Many of us can remember the flashcards we used to quiz ourselves while studying for an exam. </p><p>Some others can also recall collecting trading cards and the joy of holding them. For some, the childhood hobby <a class="Link" href="https://www.lohud.com/story/opinion/2026/01/21/ceos-can-learn-from-trading-cards-opinion/88216004007/?gnt-cfr=1&gca-cat=p&gca-uir=true&gca-epti=z114026p002950c002950e1122xxv114026d--47--b--47--&gca-ft=191&gca-ds=sophi" target="_blank" >helped forge a path to success</a>. <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2020/07/31/business/michael-dell-corner-office.html" target="_blank" >Michael Dell,</a> founder of Dell Computers; business magnate <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2010/mar/14/carlos-slim-billionaire" target="_blank" >Carlos Slim</a>, formerly the richest man in the world; and seven-time Super Bowl-winning quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://thesportsrush.com/nfl-news-were-tired-of-storing-it-tom-brady-reflects-on-his-hobby-of-collecting-trading-cards-from-age-7-to-17/" target="_blank" >Tom Brady</a>, all point to their experiences with trading cards as a formative step in their executive function.</p><p>They don't have to be the only ones holding the cards. </p><p>Innovative solutions like trading cards are the vehicle students need for proper academic development, connecting their engagement needs to the critical analog and physical play they also need to prioritize.</p><p>The positive cognitive experiences we’re witnessing across generations make it clear that trading cards play a significant role in building the skills critical for learning.</p><p>Rethinking what counts as a legitimate learning tool is long overdue. Bring trading cards into extracurricular offerings and into lesson plans. Stack the deck in the students’ favor.</p><p><i>Tisha Lewis Ellison is an associate professor in the Department of Language and Literacy Education at the University of Georgia.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-5d0000" name="module-5d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Case against man who turned in gun defies common sense
entries.summary: <p>As the Sun-Times' Frank Main <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/04/arne-duncan-education-secretary-gun-violence-cred-chicago-police-cpd" >reported</a>, Nakia Smith, a convicted felon who is not lawfully permitted to possess a firearm, entered a police station in possession of a gun, ostensibly to turn in the gun to authorities. That he had no other purpose in doing this must be acknowledged by all.</p><p>Can't the Cook County state's attorney and criminal justice system sometimes exercise some common sense and temper justice with some mercy?</p><p>And, no, I am not one of those lakefront liberals.</p><p><i>Julius L. "Jerry" Loeser, Gold Coast</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2f0000" name="module-2f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Murder case needs to be reinvestigated</h3><p>Recently, the Sun-Times ran Chip Mitchell's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/07/31/ivy-kelly-wrongful-conviction-robbins-jailhouse-interview" >story</a> about Ivy Kelly. He is serving a 30-year prison sentence. Prosecutors recently offered him a deal: If he pleaded guilty, he'd get a sentence reduction of nearly eight years and would be released immediately. He refuses to plead guilty because he says he did not commit the crime. He must remain in prison.</p><p>Mr. Kelly's case must be reinvestigated. This is certainly imperative in light of the police misconduct in investigations, which has also been reported on.<br>  <br><i>Susan Korfanty, Oak Park</i></p><h3>Costs of Trump’s scheme </h3><p>Sunday's Nation/World Associated Press story that explains Donald Trump's plan to charge readers sneak peeks to his Truth Social mentions that the scheme is illegal. </p><p>“If this was the CEO of a public company, this would be jail time,” the head of Able Alpha Trading is quoted as saying. </p><p>Our president just wants the money. We know that. But the article omits an important detail — the costs of Trump's plan.</p><p>As <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/08/01/nx-s1-5912219/trump-truth-social-access-insider-trading" target="_blank" >NPR reports</a>, "Starting Saturday, for a fee of up to $100,000 a month, trading firms can access 'Truth API' to get a glimpse of the president's often <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/05/08/nx-s1-5749358/trump-truth-social-online-posts-iran-white-house-ballroom" target="_blank" >market-moving announcements</a> about economic policy and global affairs before the rest of the world."</p><p>That is $1.2 million a year just to read the lies that flow from Trump. I am disappointed that the AP article did not start with this obscene money grab.</p><p><i>Carmel Callobre, Skokie</i></p><h3>Longing for news I can use </h3><p>I long for the days of Walter Jacobson, Floyd Kalber and Ron Magers. The news programs today are an endless litany of natural disasters, animal stories, upcoming concert events, movie openings and TV shows. Too much happy talk. Thank goodness for PBS for offering a reliable and objective source of what is going on in the real world today.</p><p><i>Eileen Carney, Palos Heights</i><br></p>

entries.title: Lake View's former Torstenson Glass building will be demolished, replaced by luxury apartments
entries.summary: <p>Two Chicago real estate companies’ plan to demolish the former Torstenson Glass building and build luxury apartments is moving forward.</p><p>North Park Ventures and SNS Realty Group first announced their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2025/08/28/sheffield-apartments-former-torstenson-glass-building-lake-view" >redevelopment project</a> for the Lake View site last summer. The companies purchased the property at 3233 N. Sheffield Ave. in July for $6.3 million, according to CBRE, who represented Torstenson Glass Co. in the sale.</p><p>The sale, and subsequent zoning change approved by the City Council in February, clears the way for the companies to turn the site into a new apartment building.</p><p>Demolition permits were issued in mid-July, city records show. </p><p>North Park Ventures said in a LinkedIn post last month that the company looked forward to starting demolition “in the coming weeks” and completing the project in 2027.</p><p>North Park and SNS Realty didn't responded to requests for interviews.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-bb0000" name="image-bb0000"></a> <picture entries.title: Dear Abby: Husband Places Blame for Everything on His Wife
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I have been living with my mom for a little over a year. Our 4-year-old lives here also. Mom has guardianship of her because of our past. A month ago, my husband decided he was leaving. I didn't leave with him because of my daughter. Now he acts like everything that was wrong in our marriage is my fault.</p><p>We are supposed to be working on our relationship. All he does is point out everything that's wrong with me. We have been together for 11 years. He says I don't put him first. I love him with all my heart. I don't know what to do. Maybe you can give me some advice? — <i>NOT ALL MY FAULT IN THE SOUTH</i></p><p><b>DEAR NOT ALL MY FAULT:</b> It is easy to assign blame to someone else, but when a marriage crumbles, rarely is it the fault of only one partner. Offer your husband an opportunity to air his grievances with you and a licensed marriage counselor. I wish you had mentioned who he feels is higher on your list of priorities than him. If it's your daughter, your priorities are ordered correctly. Not knowing the man or the "past" to which you alluded, it's possible he's looking for an excuse to leave you and start over.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have a stepson, stepdaughter-in-law and stepgrandchild. My husband and I treat them whenever we are together. Although we always pay for everything, we are never invited to their house. We host every holiday and pay for that as well. At Christmas, we host, decorate our home and a tree, and buy presents for them along with providing the holiday meal, etc.</p><p>In general, my stepfamily are nice people. However, I'm finding myself more and more annoyed with the one-sidedness of our relationship, not only the financial end but the effort as well. Last year, the gift I received from them was a handmade tree ornament I later threw out. I don't know what to do. Any advice would be much appreciated. — <i>TIRED OF ONE-SIDED RELATIONS</i></p><p><b>DEAR TIRED:</b> In some families, the parents feel it's their role to be the providers. In others, there is more reciprocity. Because you are becoming increasingly annoyed, and the son, daughter-in-law and grandchild are not your blood relatives, discuss this with your husband before your resentment builds further.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have been with my boyfriend for six years. We are in our late 40s, and we both work full time. For the past six months, he has had zero interest in showering daily. I see him do it on the weekend occasionally. He drives a semi locally and is home each night.</p><p>How does one even bring this matter up? Should I be concerned? Do I dare raise the subject, and if so, how? Maybe this shouldn't bother me, but it does. I don't want to embarrass him or hurt his feelings; I just need your advice. — <i>CONCERNED IN IOWA</i></p><p><b>DEAR CONCERNED:</b> Not everyone showers on a daily basis. Any change in a partner's behavior deserves a mention. Because this is new behavior, ask him why he has chosen to shower less often. If his hygiene needs improving, for both your sakes, you can't avoid the subject.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p>

entries.title: When Shedd Aquarium’s first beluga whales came to Chicago
entries.summary: <p>The two beluga whales lay in the belly of the cargo plane, everyone on board eager for the final leg of a journey that had begun a year and a half earlier in a pristine river splashing into Canada’s Hudson Bay.</p><p>No. 1 and No. 3, as the two female belugas were then known, were to be the star attractions at Shedd Aquarium’s new $43 million Abbott Oceanarium. As crews got the world’s then-largest indoor marine mammal pavilion ready, the whales sojourned at Point Defiance Zoo & Aquarium in Tacoma, Washington.</p><p>As the jet prepared to taxi down a snowy runway at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport in early March 1991, an unattended truck, accidentally left in drive, slammed into the underside of one of the wings, damaging the plane and leaving humans and cetaceans alike stranded until repairs could be completed 14 hours later.</p><p>When the plane finally took off a day late, the pilot climbed too steeply, jolting the tanks holding the belugas.</p><p>“It was quite a wave,” said David Casper, then a Shedd veterinarian, who was among those who spent the four-hour flight shivering in wet clothes. The animals were part of a large pod of 30 belugas at Marineland of Canada in Niagra Falls, Ontario, a closed marine park that no longer can support their care.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Heidi Zeiger / Shedd Aquarium</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>That journey — like the one <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/07/22/belugas-chicago-shedd-aquarium-marineland-canada-rescue" ><u>last month</u></a> from Toronto to Chicago — drew international attention. In part, that was because of the sheer audacity of hauling marine behemoths out of tanks and trucking them to an airport, then flying them to a new home. Like the belugas’ arrival from Marineland Canada in July, those that came in 1991 sparked protests from animal activists saying it's cruel to keep whales in “concrete tanks” — the point sharpened, those protesters said, when two Shedd belugas died within minutes of each other 1½ years after the Oceanarium opened.</p><h3>Belugas an instant hit </h3><p>In late spring, belugas by the thousands head south from their northern wintering grounds to the shallows of the Churchill River estuary in Manitoba, Canada, to feed and give birth. In the late 1980s as today, the indigenous Inuit people were allowed to hunt a small number of belugas each year as part of their traditional way of life.</p><p>Shedd made a deal with the Inuits to take two of those whales in the summer of 1989.</p><p>“We really felt like we were doing a good thing," said Ken Ramirez, then Shedd’s assistant curator and supervisor of training. "We were taking these whales that were destined to be on the dinner table for the Inuits."</p><p>Animal rights activists called the capture a “cold-water rodeo” and said it put the belugas under extreme stress.</p><p>The whales were flown from Canada to Washington state, then to Chicago. entries.title: Northbrook native Jordy is bringing ‘cool boy summer’ to Northalsted Market Days
entries.summary: <p>Jordy has a confession to make. </p><p>“Honestly, this will be my first Market Days,” he said ahead of the long-running Northalsted/Lake View street festival, which he headlines on Sunday.</p><p>Although the 31-year-old GLAAD and Queerties-nominated singer/songwriter, born Jordan Shulman, grew up in Northbrook, he “never really lived in Chicago as an adult." He left for college, majoring in English at Boston University, followed by a move to Los Angeles in 2017 to pursue his dreams of becoming a bona fide pop artist.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-cf0000" name="image-cf0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4566352/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6401x3592+0+337/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F08%2F76226f534b1e91736cccb78bae2a%2Fjordy-260808-7.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a9ee2f2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6401x3592+0+337/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F08%2F76226f534b1e91736cccb78bae2a%2Fjordy-260808-7.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f841111/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6401x3592+0+337/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F08%2F76226f534b1e91736cccb78bae2a%2Fjordy-260808-7.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="JORDY sits at Senior Citizens Memorial Park in Bucktown, Thursday, August. 6, 2026. id="module-a80000" name="module-a80000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Jordy </h3><br><b>When:</b> 9 p.m., Aug 9<br><b>Where:</b> Northalsted Market Days, Halsted Street from Belmont Avenue to Addison Street<br><b>Tickets:</b> $20 suggested donation<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://northalsted.com/" target="_blank" >northalsted.com</a></div> </div><p>That goal was met in 2019 with his breakout hit “Just Friends” and reached a fever pitch in 2023 with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/4/17/23685725/jordy-story-of-a-boy-song-northbrook-absolutely-girl-kim-petras-nine-days-john-hampson-lollapalooza" target="_blank" >“Story of a Boy,”</a> where Shulman reinterprets the lyrics of rock band Nine Days’ Y2K hit “Absolutely (Story of a Girl)” through a queer lens. The song quickly went viral after it was featured in social media posts where transgender people shared before-and-after photos of their transition. <b></b> His popularity led to appearances on “The Today Show,” “The Kelly Clarkson Show" and “Good Morning America” and garnered 350 million streams of his catalog to date. <b></b></p><p>The success of “Story of a Boy” and what it has meant to the LGBTQ community has been the lead-up to the singer’s appearance at Market Days <b></b>(and Chicago Pride Festival in 2023), and he couldn’t be happier about how his career has played out. <b></b></p><p>“Early in my career, I kept hearing this word ‘pigeonhole,’ like, ‘don’t pigeonhole yourself as the gay artist,’ but that thought hasn’t crossed my mind once,” he said. “At the end of the day, I’m an openly gay man who is very upfront about that in my music. And pride is something that adds an extra layer of importance in what I do. It’s special to be in a space like Market Days where we've all kind of shared such similar journeys. Every single one of us at some point in life felt like we didn't belong in a space and now we're making up an entire space together, and I love that.”</p><p>That journey is a recurring theme on Shulman’s fourth album, “In Retrospect,” released July 10, that he defines as a coming-of-age-at-30 project. Across 11 tracks, he looks in the rearview mirror at how far he has come personally and professionally, from the Glenbrook North theater kid who spent hours alone in his bedroom listening to pop-rock queens Avril Lavigne, Hilary Duff and Michelle Branch, to now creating queer anthems himself and finding peace with it all, even the hard moments. <b> </b>“Some of my earlier songs [on 2021’s ‘Mind Games’ and 2023’s ‘Boy’] were coming from someone who just really desperately wanted a boyfriend or a man to validate him. Now I’m turning inward and finding all of that within me," he adds. <b></b></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Jordy performs at Outloud Music Festival at WeHo Pride on June 7 in Hollywood, California.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Amy Waters</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>One of the most honest and heartfelt songs on his new album is the soft-spoken ballad “Normal People,” where Shulman comes to terms with being single and childless at an age he was sure he’d have his own version of the white picket fence. The song harkens back to a time he struggled with the idea of ever feeling “normal.”</p><p>“There’s a memory I'll always have of the first year I came out, when I was 15,” Shulman said. His mom was dropping him off at the Highland Park Community House for a summer camp reunion, and as he started crying about what being gay meant for his future, she pulled the car over to offer words of encouragement. </p><p>"She said, ‘I promise you that you will be able to have a family. You will be able to have kids, I promise you that you'll have this,’” he recalled. “I look back on that and I'm like, how lucky am I to have had a mother so loving and accepting of me? But it's also like so many of us can relate. When we were that age, we saw ourselves having those dreams by now.”</p><p>Surprisingly, Shulman was met with some negativity around the track. “It hit kind of a bad corner of the internet, and there was a lot of homophobia in the comments … some of which said it should be a woman singing it,” he said. “I think people are sometimes shocked to see a man expressing an emotional response … and I think for myself it’s been part of subconsciously redefining what being a man means.”</p><p>That’s surfaced the past couple of months as the singer’s latest social push has been centered on his new pop-rock anthem “Cool Boy” and promoting #CoolBoySummer, where he wants to shift the meaning of the label. “I never felt like a cool boy growing up. And I still don't really feel like a cool boy, to be honest,” he said. </p><p>As for what he hopes people will do in response to the hashtag: “Show me you. Show me your hobbies! Like I'm obsessed with reading and I want more boys to read. I want that to be a cool boy thing,” he said. “I want more people to talk about the s--- they like and get excited about it. Embrace who you are and don’t let anyone dim your light.”</p>

entries.title: Geraldine de Haas, who helped shape city's jazz scene, dies at 91
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Geraldine "The Jazz Lady" de Haas, who was the driving force behind the creation of the annual Chicago Jazz Festival, died July 28 from natural causes.</p><p>She was 91 and had moved from her South Side home to New Jersey 13 years ago to be closer to family.</p><p>In 1974, following jazz great Duke Ellington's death, Mrs. de Haas helped organize a tribute to Ellington in Grant Park that became an annual event and united the city's jazz community. It evolved into the city's first Chicago Jazz Festival in 1979.</p><p>Programming of the event was eventually assumed by the Jazz Institute of Chicago, leading Mrs. de Haas to focus on creating the South Shore Jazz Fest — which was held at the South Shore Cultural Center from 1981 to 2012.</p><p>"My mother's legacy in Chicago is one of great fortitude and persistence in establishing America's original art form, jazz, and making Chicago a hub of that original art form," said her son, Darius de Haas.</p><p>Mrs. de Haas said in a 2012 interview on WTTW's "Chicago Tonight" that the festival's presence in Grant Park paved the way for other festivals along the downtown lakefront.</p><p>"Jazz Fest was the catalyst for all the festivals that finally came to the city of Chicago," she said. "Everything came out of that first tribute to Duke Ellington because they saw how many people from every corner of this city gathered there to hear this wonderful music."</p><p>Mrs. de Haas was born Jan. 16, 1935, in Newark, N.J. and grew up in a family of nine kids.</p><p>In her early 20s, she teamed with her brother Andy Bey and sister Salome Bey to form a trio — Andy and the Bey Sisters — that toured the United States and Europe and for a time had a regular gig at the Blue Note in Paris. The group performed jazz and pop tunes from the late '50s to the mid '60s.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Founder of Jazz United and the driving force behind the move to build a Jazz museum, Geraldine De Haas smiles at 2255 E. 75th St. on July 24, 1998. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Bob Black/Sun-Times archive</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>She helped ensure that the 1974 tribute to Ellington was held in Grant Park and not in Washington Park on the South Side, as originally planned, so people from all different backgrounds and parts of the city would attend.</p><p>"When I first moved here I thought the city was so divided in terms of Black people on one side and white people on the other, and it seemed like the two couldn't get together," Mrs. de Haas said in a 2013 interview with WBEZ.</p><p>She marveled at how she and others persuaded city officials on the merits of holding a jazz fest near the downtown lakefront.</p><p>"Maybe it was because I wasn't from Chicago and didn't know enough to get intimidated by Chicago politics," she said. I grab hold of something and don't let go until it happens."</p><p>In addition to her son, Mrs. de Haas is survived by her daughter, Aisha de Haas.</p><p>A memorial service in Chicago is being planned.</p>

entries.title: Review: Touring production of ‘The Notebook’ is a reminder of the power of memory
entries.summary: <p>The musical version of “The Notebook” returns to Chicago, where it received its <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/10/7/23392910/the-notebook-review-chicago-shakespeare-theater-superb-romance" target="_blank" ><u>world premiere at Chicago Shakespeare in the fall of 2022</u></a>, now in a post-Broadway national tour.</p><p>I’m not quite sure whether the show has changed or I have — or more likely, a swirling combination of changes in time, cast, theater venue, expectations and more — but the show makes a different and less striking impression.</p><p>Based on the bestselling, tearjerking novel by Nicholas Sparks about a love story that begins in youth and ends in elderly dementia — made even more famous by the 2004 film version starring Ryan Gosling and Rachel McAdams — the musical has a score by multiplatinum indie singer/songwriter Ingrid Michaelson and a book by Bekah Brunstetter (Emmy-nominated producer and writer for the TV show “This Is Us”), both of which made some bold choices.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="3.0" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> ‘The Notebook’ </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-520000" name="module-520000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>When:</b> Through Aug. 16<br><b>Where:</b> Nederlander Theatre, 24 W. Randolph St.<br><b>Tickets:</b> $37-$112<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="http://broadwayinchicago.com" target="_blank" ><u>broadwayinchicago.com</u></a><br><b>Run time:</b> 2 hours and 15 minutes with one intermission</div> </div><p>Rather than a straightforward narrative, Brunstetter leaned into the conceptual frame of the story, in which the older Noah (Beau Gravitte) reads to his Alzheimer’s-afflicted wife Allie (Sharon Catherine Brown) from the titular notebook Allie wrote before she descended into complete forgetfulness. The idea is that the memories of their rocky but deep love story will “bring her back” to Noah.</p><p>Brunstetter, with help from directors Michael Greif and Schele Williams, creates a memory-scape where three versions of the couple — as teenagers (Kyle Mangold and Makena Jackson), as late twentysomethings (Ken Wulf Clark and Alysha Deslorieux) and as the elderly couple in a nursing home — move fluidly on and offstage throughout, often even sharing songs.</p><p>And those songs from Michaelson focus on the smaller, individual moments, often with characters talking (that is, singing) to themselves, trying to understand their own complex emotions more than freely expressing undying devotion or heartache.</p><p>In 2022, this thoughtful, somewhat quiet and fragmented take on time, memory, life and love came off as deeply meditative and somehow spot-on for the moment, infused with the lingering loneliness of the pandemic.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div 2x" width="490" height="275" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Alysha Deslorieux and Ken Wulf Clark portray the late twentysomething versions of Allie and Noah in “The Notebook.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Roger Mastroianni</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>To this day, I recall the quality of its wistful sentiment above all, easily forgiving all the sacrifices it made to express it. By splitting Noah and Allie each into three figures, and using cross-racial casting such that Noah and Allie were each played by a Caucasian actor at one point and a Black actor at another, the show kept us at a remove from the characters in a traditional sense. It felt purposefully archetypal and atemporal.</p><p>Then the show went to Broadway in 2024, and despite the fact that the very essence of the approach was emotional restraint, the producers sold commemorative tissue boxes for audience members to buy. The show played for about nine months, certainly qualifying as a commercial disappointment.</p><p>And now the tour feels a bit like a reversion to the Broadway mean, even the subdued songs pushing for climactic wells of emotion and ending with a rhythmic light cue. The songs used to be so clearly in Michaelson’s voice — conversational, sweetly melancholy — and now I’m not sure I’d even recognize her as so clearly hers. Even the casting has changed to be more literal — in this version, Noah is white and Allie is Black. There’s more continuity and consistency, but it’s a lot less interesting. The ending has been changed and is now less potent, more hopeful.</p><p>Still, I have a soft spot for this show, and the capable cast here delivers plenty of believable and affecting moments. As Older Noah, Gravitte carries the emotional weight of the tale with just the right sense of weathered, waning faith that Allie will recognize him. Deslorieux as Middle Allie provides a sturdy center for the love story itself, as she works through the layered complexities of hurting an innocent fiancé, disobeying parents and risking security for a passion that stings as much as it exhilarates.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Man burned to death outside Our Lady of Angels mission where nearly 100 children and nuns died in 1958 blaze
entries.summary: <p>Firefighters responding to a rubbish fire found the body of a 62-year-old man with fatal burns at the Mission of Our Lady of the Angels in the Humboldt Park neighborhood, the site where a fire ravaged a school, killing 92 children and three nuns in 1958. </p><p>At 3:05 p.m. Thursday, Chicago police officers and and firefighters were called to 3808 W. Iowa St., Mission of Our Lady of the Angels, for a rubbish fire and a tree that was on fire, according to the Chicago fire department and a Chicago police report. </p><p>The fire was out when firefighters got there, but a man, 62, who suffered burns from his knees through his upper torso, was pronounced dead on the scene at 3:15 p.m. in a courtyard of the property near the rectory, officials said. </p><p>Witnesses familiar with the man from prior encounters at the location identified him and Ring doorbell video showed him walking into the courtyard alone earlier in the day prior to the incident, according to the police report.</p><p>His name was not being formally released and an autopsy is scheduled, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>A statement from the Achdiocese of Chicago expressed condolences but referred questions about the victim to Chicago police. </p><p>"We are cooperating fully with local authorities as they investigate the death of a man near the Mission," the statement said. "We will continue to pray for the repose of his soul and for the health and safety of all members of our community," the statement said. </p><p>Area 4 detectives are investigating. </p>

class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydllejy-l-u/" target="_blank" >Robert Herguth</a></h5><p><b>Rodeo POV</b>: A man on horseback in a corral rides alongside a fleeing steer while reaching for the animal's tail, which he skillfully wraps around his right cowboy boot while maintaining a grip on the appendage. The steer twists and tumbles to the dirt. The rider — part of a so-called backyard rodeo in the far northwest suburbs last summer — gallops off, holding part of the steer's tail, which was ripped free.</p><p><b>At issue</b>: The injury is common at these types of events, according to animal rights activists who have been trying to stop what's known as steer tailing, saying it amounts to animal abuse that's illegal under state law, though seldom enforced.</p><p><b>Crackdown resistance</b>: There has been resistance to cracking down on steer tailing, called "coleadero" in Spanish, because of its place in Mexican rodeo culture dating back centuries. Sen. Li Arellano Jr. (R-Dixon), who cosponsored a stalled proposal to ban steer-tailing, says its "injury rate is higher than almost any other rodeo event," and he knows of no reputable U.S. rodeo organization that promotes steer tailing. Arellano likens steer-tailing "to cockfighting and bullfighting" and says, "The day for coleadero is over."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydllejy-l-o/" Hernandez</a></h5><p><b>Bodies discovered</b>: Fifty-seven decomposing bodies were found Thursday at South Chicago Chapel, a funeral home in South Deering, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. A funeral was in progress when police, acting on a tip, showed up. Neighbors have complained of horrible smells and questioned the late hours staff seemed to be working at the funeral home.</p><p><b>Police report</b>: Officers were met by funeral director Clark Morgan, who accompanied them on a walk-through of the building, where police found the bodies in various areas of the home, according to the police report. At some point, officers left the building, and when they tried to re-enter, Morgan locked them out and left. Officers called the fire department to get in again.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: The Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation suspended the license of the registered funeral director Johanna Morgan. Her husband previously held a funeral director and embalmer intern license, which was revoked in 2024, according to the department.</p><p><b>Identifying loved ones</b>: The Cook County medical examiner's office said it's trying to identify the remains and connect with possible descendants of the deceased. No. 1 and No. 3, as the two female belugas were known then, were flown from Tacoma, Washington, a journey that drew international attention. In part, because of the sheer audacity of hauling marine behemoths out of tanks and into trucks, then onto a plane to a new home.</p><p><b>The controversy</b>: Like the <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydllejy-l-f/" target="_blank" >belugas’ arrival from Canada in July</a>, those that came in 1991 sparked protests from activists saying it's cruel to keep whales in "concrete tanks" — the point sharpened, those protesters said, when two Shedd belugas died within minutes of each other 1½ years after the Shedd Aquarium’s new $43 million Abbott Oceanarium.</p><p><b>Looking back</b>: We took a look back at the first arrival of belugas in Chicago and talked with the people who made it happen and who protested passionately.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydllejy-l-z/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>IMMIGRATION ✶</h4><p></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="line-height: inherit; margin-top: 0px; margin-bottom: 20px; margin-left: 24px; padding: 0px; list-style-type: disc;" id="rte-a5817830-925f-11f1-9d58-d18cf2da8cda"><li><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydllejy-l-e/" target="_blank" ><b>ICE threatens Dart</b></a>: Federal immigration enforcement officials threatened to file criminal charges against Cook County Sheriff Tom Dart if he failed to comply with subpoenas asking his office to turn over detainees being held at Cook County Jail. what has become an annual tradition to raise money for Special Olympics Illinois.</p><p>Since 2005, the Chicago Ducky Derby has invited people to adopt rubber ducks starting at $10 each, with bigger sponsor packs available. The ducks are dumped into the Chicago River and head toward the finish line. The money raised helps provide year-round sports programming, adaptive equipment and other resources for athletes with intellectual disabilities.</p><p><a class="Link" native Jordy brings ‘cool boy summer’ to Market Days</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydllejy-l-ti/" target="_blank" >Selena Fragassi</a></h5><p>Jordy has a confession to make.</p><p>"Honestly, this will be my first Market Days," he said ahead of the long-running Northalsted/Lake View street festival, which he headlines on Sunday.</p><p>Although the 31-year-old GLAAD and Queerties-nominated singer/songwriter, born Jordan Shulman, grew up in Northbrook, he "never really lived in Chicago as an adult." He left for college, majoring in English at Boston University, followed by a move to Los Angeles in 2017 to pursue his dreams of becoming a bona fide pop artist.</p><p>That goal was met in 2019 with his breakout hit "Just Friends" and reached a fever pitch in 2023 when his song "Story of a Boy" went viral after it was featured in social media posts where transgender people shared before-and-after photos of their transition. His popularity led to appearances on "The Today Show," “The Kelly Clarkson Show" and "Good Morning America."</p><p>The success of "Story of a Boy" and what it has meant to the LGBTQ community has been the lead-up to the singer's appearance at Market Days (and Chicago Pride Festival in 2023), and he couldn't be happier about how his career has played out.</p><p>"It's special to be in a space like Market Days where we've all kind of shared such similar journeys," he told the Sun-Times. "Every single one of us at some point in life felt like we didn’t belong in a space and now we're making up an entire space together, and I love that."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydllejy-l-td/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>Where in Chicago are you a regular?</b></p><p>Tell us about the business that keeps you coming back — and why.</p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). entries.title: 2 hurt, including child in 4-vehicle crash involving ambulance on I-57 in Calumet Park
entries.summary: <p>Two people were hurt in a four-vehicle crash involving an ambulance late Thursday on Interstate 57 in south suburban Calumet Park. </p><p>The crash happened around 11:05 p.m. and involved an ambulance, a pickup truck and two passenger cars, Illinois state police said. </p><p>Two people were taken to area hospitals with injuries and their conditions weren’t immediately known, state police said. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://abc7chicago.com/post/4-vehicles-including-ambulance-carrying-child-involved-57-crash-calumet-park-illinois-state-police-say/19640268/" target="_blank" >ABC 7</a> reported one of the injured was a child who was in the ambulance at the time of the crash. </p><p>Inbound lanes of I-57 were shut down for an investigation and reopened just before 3 a.m., according to state police. </p><p>No further information was available.</p>

entries.title: Families, neighbors sickened by discovery of dozens of decomposing bodies at South Side funeral home
entries.summary: <p>Latasha Johnson had given the eulogy and ended her mother’s funeral service at the South Chicago Chapel, 2939 E 95th St., when she and her family noticed their vehicles were blocked in by Chicago police.</p><p>Not long after, officers found <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" >dozens of decomposing bodies</a> inside the funeral home.</p><p>“That startled me,” Johnson, 55, said. “I’m thinking maybe there’s something going on in the neighborhood, on the block, not thinking it’s something within this facility.”</p><p>Johnson was directed toward the home by her mom's hospice care providers at UChicago Medicine. She now laments not doing her research on the chapel's owners.</p><p>“I just lost my mom, they caught me at a weak point,” she said. “I trusted them with my mom’s remains. I paid them in full.”</p><p>Police, acting on a tip, went to the chapel Thursday after learning that bodies at the South Deering funeral home were not being stored at or below 40 degrees, as required by state regulations, according to a police report obtained by the Sun-Times.</p><p>Officers were met by funeral director Clark Morgan, who accompanied them on a walk-through of the building, according to the report. During the walk-through, officers found 57 bodies in various areas of the funeral home. The bodies were not refrigerated and were in various stages of decomposition, according to the report.</p><p>In a Friday statement, Illinois Comptroller Susana Mendoza said the funeral home’s operators, Johanna and Clark Morgan, were already known by the comptroller's office for their “egregious past practices while operating the Heights Crematory,” which was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/06/19/chicago-heights-crematory-bodies-death-license-closed" >a similar situation in 2025</a>.</p><p>The business’ license had been revoked Wednesday, according to the report. It was initially unclear why police didn’t visit the funeral home until the next day.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson in a Friday statement said he was "horrified" by what was happening at the funeral home and said an investigation into the operation was ongoing.</p><p>"As this investigation continues, our hearts are with every family searching for answers," he said. "We hope they receive the clarity they deserve, and the peace of mind of knowing their loved ones will be laid to rest with the dignity, care, and respect every person deserves."</p><div </div><p></p><h3>‘They need to never be opened again.’</h3><p>Outside the funeral home Friday, bodies were still being loaded into the back of vehicles, to be taken to the Cook County medical examiner's office. One neighbor teared up with her hand on her chest as she watched on.</p><p>Lakina Staples said she initially had a positive experience with the funeral home for her aunt’s funeral last month, but was visibly emotional outside the home after finding out about the bodies.</p><p>“I was sick, I had to pull myself together,” Staples, 54, said. “I’m sick to my stomach knowing that it can possibly be my auntie in that crowd.”</p><p>Staples and her family still haven’t received her aunt’s remains despite paying the home.</p><p>“They have collected a lot of money, not just from us, from everybody,” Staples said. “They need to be closed down, they need to never be opened again.”</p><p>Keith Allen Young’s family waited for hours Thursday for his body to be delivered to the church for his wake. But the body never arrived.</p><p>When relatives called South Chicago Chapel seeking answers about where their loved one’s body was, they said their calls were never returned.</p><p>“We are devastated,” said Stephanie Young, Keith Young’s older sister. “The goal is to put my brother to rest, and we have no answers from anybody.”</p><p>Keith Young died July 26. Stephanie Young said they sought the services from the funeral home because it was recommended by a friend. Now, they say they regret that decision.</p><p></p><p>Keith Young’s body was delivered to the funeral home on Wednesday, the same day the business had its license revoked. The funeral home was supposed to prepare the body and have it delivered to a church Thursday, but it never arrived. </p><p>No one contacted them to let them know it wouldn’t show up. Instead, they found out the funeral home was shut down on the news.</p><p>The funeral was scheduled for Friday. Instead, the family went to the medical examiner's office Friday morning to search for their loved one. They said they only want for Keith Young to be laid to rest.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Latasha Johnson noted an obituary made for her mother by the home used AI-generated pictures featuring individuals she didn’t know.</p><p>“I had to tell my family and friends that came by, I don’t know these people [in the pictures,]” she said.</p><p>Latasha Johnson hopes her mother and the families of others found in the home get justice.</p><p>“My mom’s body was here, but to think my mom’s body was piled on top of other decomposed bodies, that’s evil,” she said. “They need to go to jail immediately. entries.title: Boy, 17, gunned down in Austin
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for the person responsible for fatally shooting a 17-year-old boy in the Austin neighborhood Friday morning. </p><p>The teen, whose name has not been released, was found with a gunshot wound to the back of the head about 9:15 a.m. in the 4900 block of West Washington Boulevard, police said. </p><p>He was pronounced dead on the scene, according to police, and no arrests have been made. </p><p>Area 4 detectives are investigating. </p>
