entries.title: Inmigración detiene en el Midway a DJ de Sueños Festival pese a tener un caso de asilo pendiente
entries.summary: <p>Omar David Panqueva y su esposo, Santiago Páez, estaban a punto de tomar un vuelo a Washington D.C. el domingo para asistir a una serie de afterparties de Karol G tras su gira por el país.</p><p>Panqueva, conocido como DJ TUNJO, se presentó en el Sueños Music Festival en Grant Park en mayo y la pareja fundó la organización de música latina y eventos comunitarios con sede en Chicago, La Mesa Presents.</p><p>Cuando salían de un Uber para entrar al Aeropuerto Midway, los agentes federales los rodearon y detuvieron.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-be0000" name="module-be0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Silvia Paez, la hermana de Santiago, los describió en publicaciones en redes sociales como “no sólo pareja, sino un equipo poderoso”. En un comunicado dijo que la pareja había sido trasladada a un centro de detención en Indiana tras ser detenida en Midway.</p><p>“Están bien, dadas las circunstancias”, escribió en redes sociales. “Pero siguen separados”.</p><p>El Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) dijo que detuvo a la pareja por haber permanecido más tiempo del permitido con visas de 2021 que expiraron en 2022, pero no quiso decir si a los dos se les había acusado de algún delito ni si el departamento tenía conocimiento de solicitudes de asilo pendientes.</p><p>“Ambos permanecerán detenidos a la espera de audiencias de deportación”, destacó la agencia federal.</p><p>Sin embargo, su abogado, Enrique Espinoza, dijo que ambos tenían casos de asilo pendientes y que habían sido presentados dentro del plazo legal tras su llegada a Estados Unidos, pero que el gobierno “se está saltando esa parte”.</p><p>Destacó que la pareja había cooperado con el gobierno en el caso pendiente, incluso proporcionando la información biométrica requerida.</p><p>“Han sido proactivos solicitando información sobre el estado de su caso y el gobierno dijo que estaba trabajando en ello”, comentó Espinoza al Sun-Times. “Y aquí estamos ahora con ellos detenidos a pesar de que cumplieron todas las reglas del gobierno y no tienen antecedentes penales... Parece que simplemente fueron blancos fáciles”.</p><p>Una <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/help-us-free-santiago-and-david-dj-tunjo" target="_blank" >campaña de GoFundMe</a> para la defensa legal y los gastos de viaje de la pareja había recaudado más de $21,000 hasta la mañana del viernes. El abogado de la pareja no respondió de inmediato a una solicitud de comentarios.</p><p>La hermana de Páez instó a la gente a “tener cuidado” y a evitar los aeropuertos. También escribió que el apoyo y “lo mucho que la gente se está solidarizando” eran “ de las cosas que los mantienen fuertes”.</p><p>“Santiago y David están muy conscientes de cómo la comunidad los ha apoyado”, señaló la hermana de Páez. “Están muy agradecidos por todo su apoyo y su amabilidad y abrumados por el cariño que les han mostrado”.</p><p>En otra publicación en redes sociales, dijo, “Ojalá viviéramos en un mundo donde ser latino no fuera un crimen”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Kentucky recruit Jake Nawrot, one of the best quarterbacks in the country, leads No. 10 Hersey
entries.summary: <p><i>The high school football season begins on Aug. 20. The Sun-Times is counting down to kick off with previews of the top ten teams in the preseason Super 25. The series begins today with a look at No. 10 Hersey.</i></p><p>Jake Nawrot’s ascension from a normal high school football player at Hersey into <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-sports/2026/05/02/herseys-jake-nawrot-who-committed-to-kentucky-is-no-5-qb-nationally-in-2027-recruiting-cycle" >one of the best quarterbacks in the country</a> took most of the Illinois high school football community by surprise.</p><p>Josh Riggs, Nawrot’s teammate and friend, had a front row seat as Nawrot blossomed into a consensus top five national talent.</p><p>“Honestly, it has just been crazy,” Riggs said. “It was out of the blue but then it kind of wasn’t. He put that work in. He deserves every offer he got. All the attention he is getting now is a testament to the work he put in. Countless hours all when no one was looking. It showed up on Friday nights.”</p><p>Nawrot threw for a school record of 3,078 yards and 41 TDs as a junior last season. The 6-4, 200-pound Kentucky recruit is the No. 5 quarterback in the country, according to Rivals and 247sports.</p><p>“I’ve been playing quarterback since I was eight years old, but I didn’t know it was going to get this serious until sophomore offseason when I started getting recruited,” Nawrot said.</p><p>Montini’s Israel Abrams is the state’s highest-regarded quarterback. The Miami recruit is the No. 3 ranked quarterback in the country. Trae Taylor, who played for the past three years at Carmel and recently transferred to Nebraska, is the top-ranked QB in the nation.</p><p>“I know Izzy and Trae from the big QB events,” Nawrot said. “We all just blew up over time. It’s crazy how many good quarterbacks Illinois produces now. There is a lot of talent in Illinois. It is starting to become a football state.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-240000" The Huskies have the potential to reach that level and more this season.</p><p>“We have a younger team this year, and we are trying to get the troops going and rally,” Nawrot said. “We have a talented group of skill guys and have a good chance to make a run. On paper, we are really solid. We have to keep our heads down and keep working.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-hangRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bc0000" name="module-bc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>Hersey schedule</b><br><ul id="rte-bd3bc9b1-927f-11f1-a259-67d985e261d4"><li><b>Aug. 21</b> vs. Carmel</li><li><b>Aug. 28</b> at Hoffman Estates</li><li><b>Sept. 4</b> at Neuqua Valley</li><li><b>Sept. 10</b> vs. Barrington</li><li><b>Sept. 18</b> vs. Buffalo Grove</li><li><b>Sept. 25</b> at Wheeling</li><li><b>Oct. 2</b> at Elk Grove</li><li><b>Oct. 9</b> vs. Rolling Meadows</li><li><b>Oct. 16</b> at Prospect</li></ul></div> </div><p>Nawrot was a standout player for Hersey’s ranked basketball team last winter. entries.title: Bulls roster build feels like they won't be cellar dwellers in 2026-27
entries.summary: <p>Norman Powell is very well aware of his situation.</p><p>After all, the veteran Bulls guard might not be a hardened businessman, but he has been around the league long enough to understand the business.</p><p>So when he signed a two-year, $45-million contract with Year 2 being a team option, he did the team a favor because of the flexibility it allows but also did right by himself because of how fluid it keeps him on the trade front.</p><p>If the Bulls feel the need to move Powell come February, it’s essentially an expiring contract. That also means Powell likely would be sent to a contender. At age 33, it’s not a bad situation to be in, and it’s also the new mindset in the NBA.</p><p>“I just think with the way the league is and free agency, just the aprons and things like that, teams are trying to get creative,” Powell said last month. “For me, I go into every situation wanting to be here, wanting to help win and contribute anyway I can. But looking at the business of it, I’ve been around so long that those things have crossed my mind. I’ve thought about [the flexibility the deal allows], but I don’t pay too much mind on it. My focus is on being here, being in the moment, and how I can help.”</p><p>How he can help is to make sure the Bulls don’t finish in the bottom three of the league. Because of the new “3-2-1 lottery” system, the days of tanking to the basement are over. The actual sweet spot in the standings for a rebuilding team — which the Bulls certainly are — is finishing Nos. 4-10. That earns three lottery balls and an 8.1% chance at No. 1.</p><p>Just one reason the Bulls wanted a veteran such as Powell, and a rebuilding franchise like Brooklyn added Julius Randle and retained Michael Porter Jr.</p><p>It’s the new way of approaching team building. It’s like the adage about being in the woods with some people and coming across an angry bear. You don’t necessarily need to be faster than the bear. Just faster than the people you’re with.</p><p>Did executive vice president of basketball operations Bryson Graham accomplish that? That remains to be seen, but he did purchase the best running shoes available to give himself that chance.</p><p>Bottom of the NBA</p><p><b>30. Sacramento</b>: The Kings have been an absolute mess for a few seasons and don’t expect that to change this season. Zach LaVine opted in for the final year of his max deal, while Domantas Sabonis was a trade candidate but has yet to be moved.</p><p>For the Kings it’s all about rookie Darius Acuff Jr. and his development, but on paper it’s the worst roster in the league.</p><p><b>29. Memphis</b>: The Grizzlies actually started the new era of basketball last season when they began to purge the roster. Once Ja Morant was traded over the summer, the rebuild was on. The good news for Memphis is that the cupboards aren’t bare. Zach Edey showed some signs, Cedric Coward was an All-Rookie Team performer, and No. 3 overall pick Cameron Boozer might have the highest floor in the 2026 rookie class.</p><p><b>28. Milwaukee:</b> In finally moving<br>Giannis Antetokounmpo, the Bucks started their new chapter, doing so with an interesting but flawed roster.</p><p>Tyler Herro has All-Star DNA, Myles Turner can’t be as bad as he was last season and rookie Brayden Burries looks like a dude. It just feels like a car with a lot of parts that don’t necessarily fit.</p><p><b>27. Brooklyn</b>: The Nets could be the Bulls’ biggest competition for that No. 4 or No. 5 spot in the basement. Randle and Porter can play, Egor Demin had a solid second half of the season and an outstanding Summer League, while rookie Mikel Brown Jr. showed flashes in Las Vegas of becoming something special.</p><p>The Nets easily could be way better than people think.</p><p><b>26. New Orleans</b>: Is Zion Williamson finally becoming a consistently available player? He did appear in 62 games last season, which was progress. If Williamson goes back to his bad habit of sitting in street clothes with frequent visits to the training room, the Pelicans can be a bottom-three team.</p><p><b>25. BULLS</b>: Any delusions of becoming play-in eligible in Year 1 of this rebuild should be checked at the door for now, but that doesn’t mean the Bulls can’t sneak up on teams. The frontcourt has a chance to be a force on the defensive end, while Josh Giddey and Powell will be an interesting backcourt.</p><p>What helps is the Bulls also have some depth coming off the bench, which should keep them out of the bottom three.</p>

entries.title: Rating the Bears' rookies during training camp
entries.summary: <p>Tuesday night, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> rookie receiver Zavion Thomas sent veteran Kalif Raymond a video of the ankle exercises he does every night before bed.</p><p>Typically during <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/06/bears-training-camp-report-day-8-qb-caleb-williams-sharper-bryson-graham-nfl-bulls" target="_blank" >training camp</a>, it’s the other way around.</p><p>“It's a vet-type mindset to be disciplined and do something like that,” said Raymond, who is entering his 10<sup>th</sup> season in the NFL but first with the Bears. “And when he showed me that video, I was just happy to know that that's who he is.”</p><p>The speedster’s focus — he follows Raymond around like a pilot fish — is one of the most encouraging rookie developments during training camp. As the Bears' draft picks prepare for their first preseason game Aug. 15, here’s a look at some rookie training camp superlatives:</p><h3>Most pressure on him: S Dillon Thieneman</h3><h3></h3><p>The injury to fellow safety Coby Bryant has put more attention on the Bears’ first-round pick — and forced him to learn the position without on-field help from the team’s biggest free-agent addition for at least the next two months.</p><p>“Everything's starting to slow down,” Thieneman said. “Starting to pick up things, tendencies from the offense and just building more connection with the guys on defense.” </p><p>Coach Ben Johnson has noticed. When he watched film of Tuesday’s practice, he saw, for the first time, something closely resembling Thieneman’s college tape.</p><p>“You can see that play speed start to show up,” Johnson said.</p><p>Thieneman is still thinking too much. But Johnson thinks that he’ll begin to play more instinctively with more practice time.</p><h3>Biggest surprise: DT Jordan van den Berg</h3><p>The South African actually took some snaps with the first team during the Beas’ run-game drills Thursday. For someone the Bears drafted as a project, that’s remarkable.</p><p>The sixth-round pick’s physical profile and athleticism scored high on the Bears’ pre-draft evaluation sheet. Now they’re starting to notice his football instincts.</p><p>“I think we all see it on the field — that he's a really good player,” defensive end Austin Booker said.</p><h3>Most versatile weapon: WR Zavion Thomas</h3><p>Johnson plans to use Thomas split wide, in the slot and maybe even at running back. Thomas’ speed — he ran the third-fastest 40-yard dash at the NFL Scouting Combine this year — makes him Johnson’s new favorite toy.</p><p>The LSU alum slots comfortably as the Bears’ fourth wide receiver. And, if you blur your eyes, maybe their third running back.</p><p>"I'm a great athlete — I can do whatever on the football field," he said. "I can throw, too."</p><p>Training camp is where he can earn those chances.</p><p>"That comes on the meeting room first, of earning some trust to get your reps, of showing that you can be trusted when you get there," offensive coordinator Press Taylor said. “And then being able to do something with it.”</p><h3>The 2026 backup: C Logan Jones</h3><p>When the Bears drafted Jones in Round 2 out of Iowa, they swore that the plan remained for Garrett Bradbury to start this season, the last one on his contract. They’ve kept their pledge, with the eighth-year vet making every snap for the first team.</p><p>“We’re cooking right now with him out there,” Johnson said. “Really pleased with what that’s looked like.”</p><p>The Bears drafted Jones thinking he’d be their long-awaited answer at center — save for Drew Dalman’s one Pro Bowl year — in 2027. It’d likely take an injury for Jones to start before then.</p><h3>Wrong place, wrong time: CB Malik Muhammad II</h3><p>Muhammad didn’t play the slot at Texas. The Bears need a slot corner.</p><p>Kyler Gordon is hurt. His replacement, Cam Lewis, had to move to safety once Bryant was injured. When Jaylon Jones couldn’t finish Thursday’s practice, Muhammad got to play with the first team as the nickel cornerback. The fourth-round pick profiles as a backup outside corner — and seems to have the edge on the oft-injured Terell Smith in that regard. He’s learning the slot, but the Bears need help there now.</p><p>‘I want to see him go out and compete,” defensive coordinator Dennis Allen said. “I want to see him play physical in the run game. I want to see him be sticky in coverage.”</p><h3>Incomplete grade: LB Keyshaun Elliott</h3><p>The former Sun Devil has been on the Physically Unable to Perform list with a back injury since the start of training camp.</p><h3>Biggest goofball: TE Sam Roush</h3><p>The third-round pick from Stanford has to be seen up close to be appreciated: like fellow tight ends Cole Kmet and Colston Loveland, Roush has the strength and nasty streak to truck a defensive back with the ball in his hands. </p><p>The Bears couldn’t say that for sure until they put on pads Monday. Then it became obvious.</p><p>“He's a stud,” Loveland said. “He's huge, first off. Big guy, super-fast, strong. And just seeing him … with the pads on, he's going to be a weapon.”</p><p>Like Kmet and Loveland, he can be a bit silly. In Stanford tight end tradition, he took his senior year mug shot with dorky glasses, complete with tape on the bridge.</p><p>“He's fun to have in the room,” Kmet said. “We have [alums from] Stanford, Michigan, Notre Dame. it displays as a smarter room than it actually is.”</p>

entries.title: Chicago murals: Andersonville cowgirls represent lesbianism and romance
entries.summary: <p>When Ruby Bean heard the call for an Andersonville mural inspired by lesbianism, she knew the cowgirls would be perfect.</p><p>“Chicago has a rich history with cowgirls, and same with Texas,” says Bean, a Texas native. “A lot of my art has to do with capturing their histories.”</p><p>So Bean submitted her design: two cowgirls “who are in love and holding hands.” The colors of the desert at sunset behind them are also the colors from the lesbian flag, dark orange graduating down to dark pink. The white of the fence the two cowgirls lean against represents the equality sign.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“I wanted it to be really on the nose with the lesbianism,” says Bean, who lives in Edgewater. But it also needed to be subtle.</p><p>In other words, if you know, you know.</p><p>The idea was perfect for Searah Deysach, owner of feminist sex toy shop Early to Bed and the building that houses it at 5138 N. Clark St.</p><p>“I liked that it was kind of evocative of romance without being overly graphic or expectedly gay,” Deysach says.</p><p>“I thought we had an opportunity to take advantage of putting more art and more queer art into the neighborhood,” she says. Andersonville boasts a lot of botanic and butterfly murals, so “I loved how sort of random cowgirls in Andersonville seemed. I just loved her vision.”</p><p>Early to Bed celebrates its 25th anniversary this year. The shop has been at its current location since 2022.</p><p>Bean says the cowgirl on the right in her mural is a nod to her best friend’s Black and Native American heritage. The one on the left reminds Bean of the cowgirls with Southern Texas charm that she knew back home.</p><p>“She’s the sweetheart in the painting,” Bean says.</p><p>The idea of cowgirls tracks for Andersonville. It's adjacent to the Uptown neighborhood that was <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/culture-the-arts/2023/04/24/mark-guarino-books-tells-chicago-country-folk-music-history#:~:text=Not%20so%2C%20argues%20local%20journalist,the%20University%20of%20Chicago%20Press." target="_blank" >once a draw for those moving from Appalachia and other spots in rural America, bringing their country music with them</a>, according to author and Sun-Times contributor Mark Guarino in his book "Country and Midwestern: Chicago in the History of Country Music and the Folk Revival."</p><p>Bean rode her bicycle from Edgewater to paint the mural on multiple plywood panels in the back yard of Deysach’s building last fall, she says. A friend from roller derby, who also works for an art installation company, helped mount it. Bean has done roller derby since she was 8, she says, and rolls under the name Black Eyed Bean.</p><p>A scholarship to Columbia College brought Bean to Chicago from Texas in 2020, she says. She discovered murals working with her mentor and Columbia College instructor <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/murals/2026/06/05/chicago-murals-lincoln-park-cheri-charlton" target="_blank" >Cheri Lee Charlton</a>.</p><p>During the pandemic, she says, Charlton would invite students to don a mask and come outside to paint murals with her. Bean responded and began learning the trade. Now she paints murals full time.</p><p>“I did not expect it to happen, but it’s snowballed into something so wonderful, and I could not be more grateful for it,” she says.</p><p>As for the cowgirl mural, Bean says that as a lesbian herself, it was a fitting assignment.</p><p>In the end, she says, “I think that the important parts are it’s just a celebration of love and stories that are untold.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d00000" name="module-d00000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Murals and Mosaics Newsletter</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-990000" name="html-embed-module-990000"></a><div class="piano-sidebar-newsletter-murals-and-mosaics"></div> </div> </div></div> </div><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b20000" name="module-b20000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Chicago’s murals and mosaics sidebar</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/murals-mosaics" target="_blank" >Chicago’s murals & mosaics</a></h3>Part of a series on public art in the city and suburbs. <b>Know of a mural or mosaic? Tell us where, and email a photo to </b><a class="Link" href="mailto:murals@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><b><i>murals@suntimes.com</i></b></a><b>. </b>We might do a story on it.<br></div> </div><p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-d80000" name="html-embed-module-d80000"></a><div class="flourish-embed" data-src="visualisation/629878"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script></div> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Tennyson Stephens, jazz pianist who starred in cult classic film ‘Stony Island,’ dies at 83
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Tennyson Stephens was a "baaad" man. </p><p>It's how fellow musicians who heard the jazz pianist gig around Chicago in the '70s tend to describe him, especially when Mr. Stephens merged talents with legendary Chicago jazz guitarist <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2025/12/17/legendary-chicago-guitarist-phil-upchurch-collaborator-with-a-whos-who-of-musicians-dies-at-84" >Phil Upchurch</a>, who died in late 2025.</p><p>The two released the album Upchurch/Tennyson in 1975.</p><p>"Tennyson was a musical genius," said keyboardist Dale Powers, adding that Mr. Stephens, who was born in Texas but established his musical reputation in Chicago, was a major influence on Donny Hathaway and Minnie Riperton.</p><p>"Donny would be asking him 'Tenny, how'd you do this, how'd you play this chord?'" said Powers.</p><p>Mr. Stephens never became a household name, but he was a beloved staple of Chicago's music scene for years.</p><p>"Tennyson was a bad cat, just a kick-ass musician, a first-call player for Upchurch, and everybody really, because he was so bad," said friend and renowned arranger Benjamin Wright.</p><p>Mr. Stephens collaborated with many musicians, including Natalie Cole, daughter of famed crooner Nat King Cole. He wrote the hit tune "Party Lights" for her.</p><p>He was tapped to act and perform in the 1978 Chicago cult-classic film "Stony Island," which was written and directed by Chicago born filmmaker Andy Davis, who also directed "The Fugitive."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://player.vimeo.com/video/1209660957?h=09c223c5fc&app_id=122963" width="426" height="240" frameborder="0" allow="autoplay; fullscreen; picture-in-picture; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" title="Stony Island scene "Party Lights - Tennyson Stephens -- "Chi-Town" - Rae Dawn Chong -- "Scat Song" - Edward Stoney Robinson"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Davis and other musicians who starred in the film — including his brother, the guitarist Richie Davis, and singer Windy Barnes — described Mr. Stephens as quiet, kind, reserved and a "consummate professional" with a golden voice who spoke through his music.</p><p>"People were in awe of him on set because he had the qualities of Stevie Wonder in terms of his musicianship and his voice," said Andy Davis. "And he had a kind of spiritual quality about him, and he laughed a lot and was funny and was a real stylist who liked to dress in a very unique way."</p><p>Mr. Stephens, who lived in Los Angeles for the past seven years, died June 29, from natural causes. He was 83.</p><p>Beginning in the '80s, Mr. Stephens spent nearly four decades in Hawaii, where he played resorts and teamed with the singer Azure McCall.</p><p>"He was like my brother," said McCall, who also played music festivals in Sweden and Finland with Mr. Stephens.</p><p>"I could walk on stage and just start singing any key and he would come in and know exactly where it was," said McCall. "He was amazing in every style on the piano, that's what made him unique. We could go from John Coltrane to Joni Mitchell to a Broadway tune to classical," she said.</p><p>The two played a fundraiser for former President Barack Obama before his first election in 2008.<br></p>

entries.title: What would you do on your last day in Chicago?
entries.summary: <p>WBEZ’s "Say More" asked listeners to describe their perfect day in Chicago if they had to leave the city. Host Mary Dixon and co-host Patrick Smith and midday news anchor Lisa Labuz <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/say-more-with-mary-dixon-patrick-smith/2026/08/04/you-have-24-hours-left-in-chicago-what-do-you-do" >shared their itineraries</a>, and readers chimed in. Here's what they said:</p><h4>Mary Dixon</h4><p><b>Sights and experiences:</b> Sunrise at Navy Pier; skyline from Miller Beach; Montrose Harbor; Chagall windows and Nighthawks at the Art Institute of Chicago; Garfield Park Conservatory; movie at the Music Box Theater; show at Metro</p><p><b>Eats and drinks:</b> Calumet Fisheries' smoked salmon and trout; tacos at QuesaBirria Jalisco in Pilsen; coco loco sundae at Margie’s Candies; nightcap at G-Man Tavern; bánh mi at Nhu Lan</p><p></p><h4>Patrick Smith</h4><p><b>Sights and experiences:</b> Swimming at North Avenue beach; Garfield Park Conservatory; Siskel Film Center for a screening of a foreign classic like "Millennium Mambo"; Art Institute; Sox game; Empty Bottle show</p><p><b>Eats and drinks:</b> Mindy’s Bakery for a bagel, a pastry and a coffee; Omarcito’s for a catfish jibarito and a fresh juice; QXY Dumplings; Chicago-style hot dog at Jr’s Red Hots; Sundae at Margie’s Candies</p><h4>Lisa Labuz</h4><p><b>Sights and experiences:</b> Art Institute, beach, sailboat, Cubs game, show at the Metro; Empty Bottle show, FitzGerald's</p><p><b>Eats and drinks:</b> Diner breakfast; shot at G-Man Tavern; Margie's; Vito & Nick's</p><p></p><h4>WBEZ callers</h4><p><b>Cindy from Burr Ridge:</b> See Chicago from the lake on a boat</p><p><b>Flora from Norwood Park:</b> DuSable Lake Shore Drive, Buckingham Fountain, Art Institute of Chicago, Cultural Center Tiffany Dome, Tiffany Dome at the former Marshall Field’s, eat in Greektown, jazz club (Andy’s, Fitzgerald, Kingston Mines), Chicago pizza at Colletti’s</p><p><b>Asan from Edgewater:</b> Little Corner Cafe, bike down the lake, Montrose Harbor to read, Lawrence Fish Market, Italian beef in Little Italy, cake in Lincoln Square, blues night</p><p><b>Samuel:</b> Al’s Beef, polish sausage on Maxwell Street, pizza downtown</p><p><b>Cream Sherry from Rogers Park:</b> Visit parents’ grave, Water Tower, Akira, Gibson’s, Penelope’s, first set at Winter’s Jazz Club; entries.title: Just George no more. ‘Other Washingtons’ adds inclusive dimension to South Side monument
entries.summary: <p>In her new public art project, Amanda Williams is grappling with what’s in a name. Specifically: Washington.</p><p>It is, of course, the surname of America’s first president, memorialized in bronze in the South Side park named in his honor, where Williams’ latest work was unveiled Thursday.</p><p>In “Other Washingtons,” commissioned by the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/dca/supp_info/cmp/monuments_new_desc.html" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Monuments Project</u></a>, Williams looks beyond George. The work honors everyone from Harold Washington, the city’s first Black mayor, to entertainment superstars such as Denzel, Kerry and Dinah, as well as everyday Chicagoans, including Benjamin Washington, the longtime band director at King College Prep high school.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a The work adds the stories of dozens of Washingtons to an existing statue featuring the nation’s first president.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Their stories are told through words and photos on 40 colorful flags and banners that now surround <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoparkdistrict.com/parks-facilities/washington-george-washington-monument" target="_blank" ><u>the existing statue of a mounted Washington</u></a>, laid out like the ring of American flags at the Washington Monument in D.C.</p><p>“The stories don’t have to be something extraordinary in the sense of how we, in present day, think people should be kind of deified,” said Williams, the prolific 51-year-old <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/10/12/23398990/macarthur-fellows-genius-grants-2022-reuben-jonathan-miller-tomeka-reid-amanda-williams" target="_blank" ><u>local artist and architect</u></a>. “They can just be: They were important to an individual, and that individual wrote about them, and they appear on these banners.”</p><p>When she set out to create the work, Williams wanted to add context to <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoparkdistrict.com/parks-facilities/washington-george-washington-monument" target="_blank" ><u>the statue</u></a> near the corner of 51st Street and South Martin Luther King Drive, which was erected in 1904 and depicts George Washington on horseback during the Revolutionary War.</p><p>Washington, a slaveowner who did not free his slaves in his lifetime, fits squarely into the brand of founding Americans with a complicated and contradictory story whose public glorification was reevaluated in recent years by the city’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/dca/supp_info/cmp/monuments_new_desc.html" target="_blank" ><u>monuments project</u></a>.</p><div </div><p>Still, Williams said, “you don’t get a fuller understanding of where we are today and why we’re in the current political climate if you begin erasing everyone who was problematic or detrimental.”</p><p>So, George remains. But now, he’s joined by a plethora of fellow Washingtons — some of whom were suggested by neighbors through a crowdsourcing effort.</p><p>“You get to first encounter these other Washingtons, and oh yeah, by the way, George,” Williams said. “So he doesn’t go away, but he's not central anymore. I think that’s a beautiful kind of response to the challenge of how do you complicate a story? How do you expand a story?”</p><p>“Other Washingtons,” which Williams has been working on for about three years, is one piece of the city’s larger <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/dca/supp_info/cmp/monuments_new_desc.html" target="_blank" ><u>monuments project</u></a>, launched in 2020 in the wake of the murder of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer and the broader racial reckoning that followed. class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Benjamin Washington, the longtime band director at King College Prep high school, is among the people honored in the new project. Jon Burge; and now, unveiled Williams’ project.</p><p>“This piece symbolizes that we can always create space for more stories, more voices, and more perspectives. entries.title: Condenan a 30 meses de prisión a hombre que disparó cerca de agentes de inmigración en operativo en La Villita
entries.summary: <p>Un juez federal sentenció a un hombre a 30 meses de prisión después de que admitiera haber disparado un arma "en proximidad de" agentes de la Oficina de Aduanas y Protección Fronteriza (CBP) durante los últimos días del Operativo Midway Blitz el otoño pasado.</p><p>Al sentenciar a Héctor Gómez el jueves, el juez de la Corte de Distrito de Estados Unidos, Matthew Kennelly, dijo que sus acciones podrían haber derivado en un desenlace mucho más trágico.</p><p>Kennelly subrayó la gravedad de las acciones de Gómez el 8 de noviembre, al afirmar que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/04/28/hombre-admite-haber-disparado-arma-cerca-de-agentes-fronterizos-durante-operativo-en-la-villita" target="_blank" >disparar un arma</a> en una "situación potencialmente volátil" podría haber puesto en riesgo tanto a los manifestantes como a los agentes federales. "Es estupendo que no haya ocurrido, pero es una situación realmente mala", dijo Kennelly.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f40000" name="module-f40000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Por esas razones, Kennelly sentenció a Gómez a 30 meses de prisión, con un año de libertad supervisada, aunque probablemente será deportado a México tras salir de prisión.</p><p>La sentencia de Gómez es la primera en un caso criminal no migratorio derivado de la campaña de deportaciones de la administración de Trump en el área de Chicago el año pasado. Gómez se declaró culpable en abril de poseer ilegalmente un arma siendo convicto.</p><p>Los fiscales federales han acusado a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >33 acusados</a>de delitos no migratorios vinculados al Operativo Midway Blitz. Veinticuatro fueron exonerados; a otros cinco se les prevé que se les retiren los cargos. Contra dos personas los cargos aún estaban pendientes.</p><p>El abogado de Gómez, Michael Monaco, pidió al juez imponer una pena de 18 meses, diciendo que Gómez lamentaba sus actos y que su juicio había sido afectado por el alcohol.</p><p>Monaco dijo que el tiroteo ocurrió durante uno de varios episodios de "consumo excesivo de alcohol" de Gómez, de 46 años, quien comenzó a beber a los 14 años. Según sus abogados, Gómez estuvo bebiendo la noche anterior y reanudó el consumo apenas se despertó la mañana del incidente.</p><p>La fiscal federal adjunta Jill Bhalakia dijo que Gómez conducía bajo la influencia del alcohol cuando disparó al menos dos veces cerca de agentes de la Patrulla Fronteriza en la cuadra 2400 al surdeKedzie Avenue.</p><p>Los fiscales agregaron que Gómez huyó del lugar antes de estacionarse cerca de la cuadra 3100 al oeste de 26th Street. Alrededor de las 2:30 p.m., Gómez salió se bajo de la Jeep, mostró el arma frente a una persona no identificada y "se rió profusamente" mientras lo hacía.</p><p>Posteriormente, la Policía de Chicago encontró a Gómez sentado en el asiento del conductor con el arma en el regazo y botellas de cerveza en la consola central, según los fiscales.</p><p>Bhalakia dijo que Gómez ha sido deportado de los Estados Unidos varias veces, fue condenado por entrada ilegal en 2010 y fue objeto de una orden final de expulsión el 10 de diciembre. Señaló que también fue condenado el año pasado por posesión ilícita agravada de un arma.</p><p>Aunque Kennelly reconoció que Gómez tenía un problema con la bebida, dijo que no había garantía de que no "se volviera a encontrar en este tipo de situaciones".</p><p>Kennelly señaló que consideraba sorprendentemente baja la pena recomendada de 30 meses dada la gravedad de la conducta de Gómez, pero dijo que respetaría la recomendación de los fiscales y no aumentaría la sentencia.</p><p>Gómez se dirigió a Kennelly durante la audiencia de sentencia, diciendo que estaba "avergonzado" y "arrepentido" de sus acciones. Comentó que su tiempo en prisión le había dado la oportunidad de reflexionar sobre la situación y que "ahora soy una mejor persona".</p><p>Gómez agregó que cuando regrese a México se reunirá con su esposa y sus tres hijos.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>
entries.author: Cindy Hernandez

entries.title: Bears sign veteran safety Xavier Woods
entries.summary: <p>Desperate for help at safety after Coby Bryant hurt his left knee earlier this week, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> signed Xavier Woods to a one-year deal Friday.</p><p>Woods certainly has the experience — he's started a whopping 121 games in nine NFL seasons. He was drafted by the Cowboys in Round 6 in 2017, playing for four seasons before signing with the Vikings in 2021. After one season in Minnesota, he played three years in Carolina and one in Tennessee. He had two interceptions in 10 starts with the Titans last year. Just two seasons ago, he played every single down for the Panthers.</p><p>He has 15 career picks.</p><p>Injuries have piled up at the position during <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/07/bears-training-camp-rookies-draft-pick-rate-superlatives-nfl-dillon-thieneman-zavion-thomas-malik-muhammad-jodan-van-den-berg" target="_blank" >training camp</a>. Bryant's injury will keep him out 8-10 weeks. Elijah Hicks began training camp on the Physically Unable to Perform list because of shin issues. Gervarrius Owens was carted off the field Thursday after hurting his leg during a punt drill. Cam Lewis, who had been filling in for the injured Kyler Gordon at slot corner, moved to Bryant's position, where he has been paired with Dillon Thieneman, the Bears' first-round pick. </p><p>Woods, 31, mostly has played free safety during his career. </p><p>To make room, the Bears put cornerback Dallis Flowers on injured reserve. He left practice Thursday.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: White Sox send C Joey Bart, LHP Chris Murphy to injured list; recall C Edgar Quero, RHP David Sandlin
entries.summary: <p>It was a heck of an upgrade while it lasted.</p><p>Sure, let’s go with that.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> put newly acquired catcher <b>Joey Bart </b>on the 10-day injured list with a fractured left hand after he was hit by a pitch Thursday in Boston in his third appearance since being acquired at the trade deadline. Back up to the big club is <b>Edgar Quero</b>, owner of a miserable .194 batting average and an even worse OPS of .492. Bart is out indefinitely.</p><p>Also sidelined after appearing in the finale in Boston — a 12-11, 13-inning wild one as the home nine completed a three-game sweep — is lefty reliever <b>Chris Murphy</b>. He goes to the 15-day injured list with a flexor strain. The Sox recalled right-hander <b>David Sandlin</b>, their No. 7-ranked prospect according to MLB.com.</p>
entries.author: Steve Greenberg

entries.title: Coming off 'unacceptable' performance last season, Bears' defense is vulnerability until it proves otherwise
entries.summary: <p>It’s always prudent to rein in the optimism when it comes to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>. Four decades of high expectations crashing down ought to be enough to learn that lesson.</p><p>It’s never popular to deliver that message, of course, and now seems like especially bad timing. The team is fresh off its first playoff win in 15 years, quarterback Caleb Williams’ stardom is surging and coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a> has a wealth of credibility in the bank.</p><p>But what about that defense?</p><p>It’s the vulnerability that few outside Halas Hall seem willing to acknowledge after a misleading performance last season. The Bears led the NFL with 33 takeaways, which was the only way they possibly could’ve masked that they were downright bad otherwise.</p><p>That’s not masked inside the building, though.</p><p>The checklist of what a good defense must do begins with stopping the run and rushing the passer. The Bears allowed the sixth-most yards rushing last season at 134.5 per game and had the seventh-fewest sacks at 35 despite defensive end Montez Sweat putting up 10 in what Johnson called the best season of his career.</p><p>“Outside of takeaways, we finished bottom-10, bottom-five in a lot of categories, so we ain’t done a damn thing,” star cornerback Jaylon Johnson said. “There’s a lot for us to prove on defense.”</p><p>There sure is. And it could be tougher for defensive coordinator Dennis Allen this season after some good talent went out the door as the Bears tried to thread the needle of trying to upgrade while also shedding some salary-cap dollars to get under the cap.</p><p>Those moves put the Bears in a familiar position: Asking everyone to trust them.</p><p>Starting safeties Kevin Byard, an All-Pro, and Jaquan Brisker were replaced by Coby Bryant and first-round pick Dillon Thieneman. Bryant was a good signing, but he had a significant knee injury this week and likely is out until October, and Thieneman, like any rookie, is an unknown until he shows something during the season.</p><p>The Bears also continue to have concerns about Kyler Gordon (injuries) and Tyrique Stevenson (attentiveness) at corner, where Johnson is the only sure thing as long as he’s healthy. Johnson and Gordon missed most of last season.</p><p>At linebacker, the Bears return T.J. Edwards, who turns 30 next week, to play with Devin Bush, who is lightning fast compared to Tremaine Edmunds, but is on his fourth team in five seasons.</p><p>The biggest problem, however, is the same one that has hurt the Bears throughout the Ryan Poles era: It’s almost impossible to thrive defensively without a pass rush, and their defensive line is Sweat and a lot of uncertainty.</p><p>Dayo Odeyingbo had one sack in eight games last season and is coming off a torn Achilles, Austin Booker is unproven and Shemar Turner is still recovering from a torn ACL. Grady Jarrett was banged up most of last season and now he’s 33. Gervon Dexter, a former second-round pick, has been good when the Bears needed him to be great.</p><p>Sweat appeared to pull a muscle in practice Thursday, further depleting the Bears at a crucial spot.</p><p>And even if the Bears had some hope of duplicating the unlikely formula that worked for them last season, 23 of those takeaways were by players no longer with the team. There’s no guarantee someone else can step up and replace that.</p><p>There are questions at all three levels of the defense, and the Bears have no option at this point but to find answers within.</p><p>If they don’t, it likely will undercut whatever progress Williams makes.</p><p>“The offense is rolling, but we [can’t] rely on, ‘OK, the offense go put up 40 and we’ll hold [the opponent] to 35,’” Jaylon Johnson said. “That’s unacceptable.”</p><p>He then ran through many of the aforementioned concerns, seeming to say they’re valid, and said, “We’ve still got a lot to do and a lot to prove. Go down the list... We’ve got a lot of people that are motivated and we’ve got to go out there and play.”</p><p>The Bears were 29th in total defense last season and were one of only two teams in the bottom 12 to have a winning record. They won games in which they allowed 42, 28 and 27 points — all three requiring a late comeback.</p><p>Playing that way ties Ben Johnson’s hands as the offensive play caller, too, because it’s hard for a team to run its way back into a game. The ripple effect will be Williams spending much of the game dropping back against a defense that knows the Bears have no choice but to pass.</p><p>When the Bears or analysts bring up the overall discouraging defensive numbers from last season, they aren’t dismissing the takeaways. They’re simply saying that’s a volatile part of the game and no defense should assume them as part of its plan.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Third grade teacher sexually abused 5 students 'multiple' times in West Chicago, prosecutors allege
entries.summary: <p>A DuPage County judge on Friday ordered a former West Chicago third grade teacher detained after he was accused of sexually abusing five students multiple times over the 2025-2026 school year, county officials announced Friday.</p><p>Mario Garcia, 54, of Aurora, was charged with two counts of predatory criminal sexual assault of a child, five counts of aggravated sexual abuse and four counts of aggravated battery, according to a statement from the DuPage County state's attorney's office. </p><p>Following a thorough, child-sensitive investigation, it was alleged that during the 2025-2026 school year, Garcia inappropriately touched five students on multiple occasions at Currier Elementary school, 800 Garys Mill Rd. the statement said. </p><p>West Chicago police and the DuPage County Children’s Center were notified by authorities on May 14 of the allegations against Garcia, a third grade teacher. </p><p>Garcia, of the 2500 block of Looking Glass Court in Aurora, remains in custody and is due back in court on Aug. 31.<br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Darren Bailey's running mate maintains abortion is 'sin against God'
entries.summary: <p>Republican candidate for Illinois governor Darren Bailey has dialed back his stance on abortion, even omitting it from his policy platform. But that hasn’t stopped the downstate farmer and former GOP legislator from campaigning on it.</p><p>Bailey and his running mate, Aaron Del Mar, spoke at a “Save America” rally in Springfield this week. The event was sponsored by anti-abortion organization Illinois Family Action, the political arm of the Illinois Family Institute, which regularly lobbies against bills expanding abortion access in Springfield.</p><p>During his six minute-speech, Del Mar railed against Illinois abortion laws, saying Gov. JB Pritzker, who is running for a historic third-term, is “willing to murder millions of babies.”</p><p>“Nobody wants to make Illinois a Mecca for abortions from everyone around the country to come here and sin against God,” Del Mar said, drawing applause from the audience.</p><p>But the Cook County GOP chairman said, in a July interview with WBEZ as part of a media tour promoting his slate’s economic policies, that abortion is not on their legislative agenda this time around.</p><p>“No matter how many times JB Pritzker and the Democrat majority try to say that Darren and Aaron are going to try to take away women's access to reproductive care, that is a flat-out lie,” Del Mar said.</p><p>Bailey and Del Mar’s campaign did not return requests for comment.</p><p>In a statement, Pritzker’s campaign spokesperson said Bailey and Del Mar are focused on “spreading the extreme MAGA agenda by attacking women’s right to choose, supporting Trump’s failing economic agenda, and spreading far-right conspiracy theories.”</p><p>Bailey faces an uphill battle, once again, as he faces off with incumbent and self-funded billionaire Pritzker. In his bid against Pritzker in 2022, Bailey leaned more into his conservative stances on social issues, including restricting abortion access, expanding gun rights and notoriously referring to Chicago as a “hellhole,” which he apologized for earlier this year.</p><p>He lost handily to Pritzker, severely underperforming in Cook County and the collar counties.</p><p>Del Mar said Bailey has changed their public-facing campaign after “learning from his mistakes from four years ago,” and they are instead focusing on affordability.</p><p>“We're talking about core services,” Del Mar told WBEZ last month. “We're not talking about abortion, we're not talking about transgender issues.”</p><p>Illinois Family Action withheld its endorsement of Bailey during the March primaries, despite donating to his 2022 campaign. The group, instead, endorsed conservative think tank President Ted Dabrowski, who lost to Bailey by 24%.</p><p>Yet, IFA invited Bailey and Del Mar, along with Republican candidate for U.S. Senate Don Tracy, who recently <a class="Link" href="https://ipmnewsroom.org/gop-u-s-senate-candidate-don-tracy-talks-abortion-ice-shootings-and-iran-war-on-21st-show/" target="_blank" >told Illinois Public Media</a>, “I do not support nationalizing abortion law.”</p><p>And in May, Bailey spoke at a Christian conference in Decatur, where he said “Anyone who knows me knows there’s no one here more pro-life or more pro Second Amendment than I.”</p><p>General elections take place Nov. 3.</p><p><i>Mawa Iqbal covers state government and politics for WBEZ. Follow @mawa_iqbal</i></p>
entries.author: Mawa Iqbal

entries.title: K9 guards stood by as fare evader pushed woman, breaking her leg at Red Line station: lawsuit
entries.summary: <p>Private security guards stood by last year, appearing to do nothing, as a CTA fare evader knocked over a 61-year-old nurse, fracturing her leg, according to a lawsuit.</p><p>The woman is still struggling with pain from the incident at the 95th Street Red Line station, which raises questions about the effectiveness of private K9 security guards, who in this case were standing nowhere near the gates to deter fare evaders, the woman's lawyer, Ken Hoffman, told the Sun-Times.</p><p>"The whole notion behind their contract is to provide a strong deterrent force. But they weren't standing near the turnstiles," Hoffman said.</p><p>The CTA last year awarded an $89 million, two-year contract to Action K-9 Security, the main defendant in the lawsuit filed in Cook County court in January. The lawsuit claims negligence against the company and its subcontractor First American Security, who employed the guards who allegedly failed to deter the fare evader.</p><p>The company's guards were standing nearby but, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w6Tn2zfU2tc" target="_blank" >security</a> <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BXJTmnJYcss" target="_blank" >videos</a> shared by Hoffman, did not appear to be aware or immediately respond to the crime happening just feet away from them.</p><p>The incident happened the morning of July 10, 2025, as plaintiff Hilary Thorne made her way to work at Stroger Hospital, according to the lawsuit.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Security video shows a man push a woman to the ground, and security guards standing to the left, at the 95th Street Red Line station on July 10, 2025.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>CTA video provided by lawyer Ken Hoffman</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Before she tapped herself and her bicycle through the accessible gate, a man asked if she could tap him in too, Hoffman said. But, because of her pass, she was unable and said she could not, Hoffman said. Security video shows her walk through the gate and try to close it as the man pushes the gate, knocking her to the ground.</p><p>A guard who appeared to notice the fare evader earlier turns his back to the turnstiles in the seconds before Thorne was pushed to the ground, the videos show.</p><p>The guards eventually walked after the man and escort him out of the station, Hoffman said. But the damage was already done to Thorne, who broke her leg and, as a result of being immobile, developed a blood clot she's still recovering from, Hoffman said.</p><p>Thorne was unable to work full time for around half a year, Hoffman said. She's still dealing with leg pain, and now worries about her safety after naming herself in the public lawsuit, Hoffman said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/w6Tn2zfU2tc?start=82&feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="BATTERY CUSTO 10 Jul 25 Redline 95th C163B JJ328107"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Action K-9 Security is now the main privately contracted security force for CTA after the agency fired its other unarmed guards earlier this year. Action K-9's contract says their purpose is to act as a deterrent for potential criminals and fare evaders, Hoffman said.</p><p>Hoffman said the guards are instructed not to intervene, although they are allowed to hold someone as any Good Samaritan would be allowed to.</p><p>"They say they have a hands-off policy. For $89 million, they should be doing more," Hoffman said.</p><p>In a statement, Action K-9 Security said "we categorically deny the allegations and provide that the allegations being reported do not accurately represent all the facts. We have denied the allegations, continue to do so and will defend the allegations in court. Every day, millions of citizens travel safely through the City of Chicago, in large part due to the security we provide," the company said.</p><p>The CTA and subcontractor First American Security did not immediately reply to a request for comment.</p><p>The CTA was initially a defendant in the lawsuit when it was filed last September, but the judge later dismissed the agency from the case due to a state immunity law that absolves the CTA of liability for crimes that happen on its property. Hoffman filed the case again in January against the security companies.</p><p>The CTA has increasingly relied on private security to patrol its trains and stations in recent years. The CTA reintroduced K9 guards in 2022, signing a $55 million, 18-month deal with Action K-9 to address rising crime on the system, according to <a class="Link" href="https://webapps1.chicago.gov/vcsearch/cta/vendors/ec90e873725f78e08c055c6509fbac903ad03a72/contracts" target="_blank" >city records</a>.</p><p>As transit crime began rising again — culminating last fall with a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/12/19/president-trump-chicago-cta-crime-security-funding-cut-mayor-brandon-johnson" target="_blank" >funding threat</a> from the Trump administration last fall — the CTA boosted patrols by Chicago police and, for the first time in recent memory, had Cook County sheriff's deputies patrol the system. The CTA said in December it was adding dozens of K9 patrols to its system.</p><p>In April, the CTA fired its privately-contracted, unarmed security guards, and said it was redirecting the money toward other trained professionals “better equipped” to keep riders safe, including K9 units.</p><p>Action K-9 Security's current contract ends in February 2027.</p><p>Hoffman said a trial date has not been set.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/7d/aa/5c95094145db9a777ccc2353ffb3/2025l011557.pdf" target="_blank" ><i>Read the lawsuit</i></a><i>:</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/7d/aa/5c95094145db9a777ccc2353ffb3/2025l011557.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Jalapeños vinculados a brote de salmonela en el país rastreados hasta un campo y distribuidor de México
entries.summary: <p>(AP) — Los chiles jalapeños vinculados a un <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/chipotle-jalapeno-salmonella-outbreak-investigation-feecdd5ba46237c8992e41de8ea6d1df" target="_blank" >brote de salmonela que afectó a varios estados</a> fueron rastreados hasta un productor en Sinaloa, México, informaron autoridades federales.</p><p>Al menos 345 personas en 27 estados, incluyendo Illinois, han sido reportadas como enfermas por la cepa de salmonela vinculada a los jalapeños. La mayoría se han registrado en Minnesota y Colorado. No se han reportado muertes, pero las autoridades dicen que 36 personas han sido hospitalizadas.</p><p>Los Centros para el Control y la Prevención de Enfermedades (CDC) dijeron el miércoles que los chiles jalapeños fueron introducidos en Estados Unidos por el distribuidor Coast Citrus Distributors. La empresa ha retirado del mercado los chiles y está notificando a sus clientes, que incluyen a algunas cadenas destacadas de restaurantes de comida mexicana, informaron los funcionarios.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-0f0000" name="module-0f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Coast Citrus Distributors no respondió de inmediato a un mensaje de voz dejado el jueves en busca de comentarios.</p><p>La Administración de Alimentos y Medicamentos (FDA) dijo que, de las 191 personas entrevistadas en la investigación del brote, 177 —o el 93%— informaron haber comido en un restaurante de estilo mexicano, entre ellos Chipotle Mexican Grill y Qdoba, entre el 14 de junio y el 14 de julio.</p><p>Chipotle Mexican Grill notificó el martes que había retirado los jalapeños de algunos de sus restaurantes. Qdoba dijo el miércoles que la compañía había retirado de manera proactiva los jalapeños de todos sus restaurantes.</p><p>"Dadas sus acciones para retirar el producto de sus tiendas, ninguno de estos establecimientos se considera un riesgo actual y continuo para los consumidores en este brote", informaron los funcionarios del CDC.</p><p>La FDA está investigando si algunos de los jalapeños llegaron a supermercados. La agencia podría anunciar más medidas en su página de retiros y alertas, dijeron funcionarios de salud.</p><p>Las bacterias Salmonella causan unas 1.35 millones de infecciones en Estados Unidos cada año, y los brotes se han vinculado a fuentes como pepinos, huevos, leche sin pasteurizar, albahaca fresca, gecos y dragones barbudos como mascotas.</p><p>Dentro de horas o días tras la exposición a las bacterias, las personas infectadas pueden sufrir diarrea, fiebre y cólicos estomacales. La enfermedad suele durar de cuatro a siete días, y la mayoría de las personas se recupera sin tratamiento.</p><p>Los niños pequeños, los adultos en edad de jubilación y las personas con sistemas inmunitarios debilitados tienen un mayor riesgo de sufrir una enfermedad más grave, según los CDC.</p><p>Las acciones de Chipotle, con sede en Newport Beach, California, cayeron casi un 10% el martes y no se han recuperado. Varias cadenas de comida rápida casual, como Chipotle, han registrado menos afluencia de clientes de ingresos medios y bajos debido a la inflación general en Estados Unidos, y los titulares recientes sobre <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/cyclospora-lettuce-taco-bell-restaurants-customers-39083c579b4ba7d3d5d8a23ea3fd5b00" target="_blank" >enfermedades transmitidas por alimentos</a> pueden ser otro factor negativo.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Questions remain as Welch discusses Benton harassment case
entries.summary: <p>Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/05/welch-benton-harassment-working-group-cassidy" >sat down for interviews</a> with selected reporters last week. He told most of them that his office had conducted an “informal investigation” into sexual harassment allegations against former Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield, in 2023.</p><p>Welch’s staff has not responded to our request for an interview (same goes for the Chicago Tribune). But nobody asked whether he and his staff spoke to anyone other than Benton and the 22-year-old district office staffer who accused Benton of sexual harassment during that informal investigation after she’d resigned to avoid more harassment. Benton <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/07/03/plainfield-state-rep-harry-benton-resigns-amid-allegations-of-misconduct" >resigned</a> last month.</p><p>Jessica Dixon Heitman also worked in Benton’s office at the time and has said she left because of the treatment of the young woman. But as far as I can tell, nobody talked to her in 2023. Heitman was recently appointed to replace the disgraced Benton.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-700000" name="module-700000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>So based on talking to just two people, Welch concluded that this was a "he said, she said" dispute, and, therefore, since no formal complaint was filed, Benton “was entitled to a constitutional right to due process,” Welch told WGN TV. “I had to support a member, and I supported a member.” His caucus committee contributed $1.4 million to Benton’s reelection campaign.</p><p>Set aside for a moment the constitutional right to receive $1.4 million in campaign contributions after an overly narrow informal probe. Welch also told WGN, “We had to respect the wishes of the survivor, even though she didn't want to go through a formal complaint process.”</p><p>However, as the Tribune has reported, the accuser’s main reason for coming forward was to make sure that no other woman would be harassed by Benton.</p><p>At least two more women were sexually harassed by Benton after that, according to the legislative inspector general.</p><p>And despite what Welch reportedly told the House Democratic Women’s Caucus last month and then WGN last week, the Illinois AFL-CIO issued a remarkably forceful response to a question I asked by releasing a statement saying, “Any suggestion that Harry Benton — or any elected official — controlled labor's support for a candidate or caucus is false.”</p><p>Last month, I informed my subscribers that Welch told members of the Women’s Caucus, “Harry Benton went around telling union people that the speaker retaliated against him and should have given more support in his last [2022] race,” a member paraphrased Welch’s response at the time.</p><p>The Tribune reported last week that the newspaper learned from participants in the meeting that “Welch assisted the now-disgraced former lawmaker’s 2024 reelection campaign with $1.4 million to prevent Benton from actively working to curb organized labor support to the speaker’s war chest.”</p><p>And Welch told WGN last week that, while he regretted supporting Benton, “labor was a big advocate of Rep. Benton. As a union member himself, he had a lot of support.”</p><p>Some folks I talked to said it looked like Welch was throwing labor under the bus, so I reached out to the Illinois AFL-CIO and asked for its reaction to last week’s stories.</p><p>“The Illinois AFL-CIO has no tolerance for sexual harassment, in the workplace or anywhere else,” the labor umbrella organization declared. “We were deeply disturbed by the legislative inspector general's report and by recent reporting on former Rep. Harry Benton's egregious conduct, and we agree with his decision to resign. Any suggestion that Harry Benton — or any elected official — controlled labor's support for a candidate or caucus is false. It is clear the General Assembly needs to take further action to strengthen its policies and procedures to combat harassment and support the brave victims who come forward.”</p><p>The Tribune also quoted some Democrats close to organized labor who accurately noted that “Benton had little power to influence organized labor or its massive fundraising apparatus.”</p><p>Labor did support Benton in 2024, and a big reason was that Benton’s Republican opponent was Gabby Shanahan. At the time, Shanahan worked for the anti-union Illinois Policy Institute. I’ve written several times (including in my syndicated newspaper column in 2024) that there was no way on this earth that organized labor wanted an Illinois Policy Institute staffer in the General Assembly. Shanahan is running again this year, but she no longer works for the Illinois Policy Institute.</p><p>Now, a question could be asked about what would’ve happened if Welch or someone in his organization had told union leaders about the 2023 sexual harassment allegations against Benton by a 22-year-old district staffer.</p><p>But remember, Welch’s “informal investigation” included talking to only Benton and the staffer. And then the matter was closed.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c80000" name="module-c80000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: CPS moves further from funding adequacy despite getting more state dollars
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Public Schools need about $1.9 billion more from the state in order to provide an adequate education, a gap that has grown over the past two years, according to data released Friday by Illinois education officials.</p><p>The news will immediately bolster growing calls for the state to give the city’s school district more money. CPS faced a $732 million deficit this year, and just last week, the school board approved a budget that included hundreds of staff cuts in central office and classrooms.</p><p>A majority of board members sought to lessen those cuts by backing a revised budget — against the wishes of Supt. Macquline King — that assumes $150 million more from the state. After passing that budget in a controversial split vote, they vowed to go to Springfield during the November veto session to pressure lawmakers to come up with the funding.</p><p>CPS is not alone. Out of about 940 school districts in Illinois, 714 have moved further away from adequacy this school year. Each district’s funding target is determined by considering student demographics such as poverty and measuring how much money would be needed to have minimum ratios of students to teachers, counselors and other central staff.</p><p>While funding has gone up overall — this year, as has happened most years under Gov. JB Pritzker, funding through the state's formula went up by $350 million — many factors have caused the state to fall increasingly short, including that costs have risen.</p><p>CPS now only has 70% of what it needs to provide an adequate education, down from 73% last year and 79% the year before. And the number of school districts across the state with 70% or less than what they need doubled in the past year.</p><p>The Illinois Federation of Teachers said in a statement that it is “clear that Gov. JB Pritzker and state lawmakers must correct the bare-minimum approach to school funding that is currently failing students, educators, and communities across Illinois.”</p><p>"Today's report should serve as a wake-up call," said Stacy Davis Gates, president of the Illinois Federation of Teachers and the Chicago Teachers Union. "A child entering kindergarten today will graduate from a high school that is still underfunded.”</p><p>A 2018 law changed the way Illinois distributed money to school districts and established the adequacy target. The law called for the state to increase funding by a minimum of $300 million a year and set a goal of having all school districts funded to 90% adequacy by 2027.</p><p>But Illinois has fallen way behind. The state would need to contribute nearly $6 billion more to make all schools adequate. At the current rate, it will take another 14 years, according to the state.</p><p>Pritzker’s office did not respond to Friday’s release by the Illinois State Board of Education. He has repeatedly pointed out that public education funding has increased by $3 billion under his administration.</p><p>State Supt. of Education Tony Sanders said on a call with the media Friday that every school district will receive more funding this year. He also made the case that the state contribution wasn’t the problem, nor was the funding formula, which he said was “working.”</p><p>He said many factors are causing school districts to move further away from adequacy. Chief among them: The state changed the way it was counting the number of poor students, which led the needs of every district to grow since the formula calls for school districts with more poor children to get more money.</p><p>And costs went up, including for salaries. There was also a significant decrease in revenue from a state tax on corporations, Sanders said.</p><p>When asked if all those factors should lead to the state putting more into education funding, Sanders pointed out that “we've made record investments in public education, while many other states have not made similar investments.”</p><p>House Speaker Chris Welch did not respond to questions, but he recently said he wanted to provide more money for CPS — though he has not offered details.</p><p>Senate President John Harmon’s office responded that there’s “no greater supporter of public education than the Senate Democratic Caucus.”</p><p>"The Senate President looks forward to working with our allies and partners to identify resources to continue increasing our investment in students each year,” said John Patterson, spokesman for Harmon, in a statement. “We also hope our partners in Washington recognize that continued federal investment in public education is essential at a time when states are being asked to do more with increasing fiscal uncertainty."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul entries.title: Owners of Far South Side funeral home have history of mishandling human remains
entries.summary: <p>The discovery of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" >over 50 decomposing bodies</a> in a South Deering funeral home was not the first time its business’ operators were found to have mishandled remains.</p><p>Last year, state officials <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/06/19/chicago-heights-crematory-bodies-death-license-closed" >shut down a Chicago Heights crematory</a>, also operated by Clark and Johanna Morgan, amid allegations they had mishandled over 100 bodies at the facility.</p><p>That business was permanently shut down by state officials and nearly two dozen lawsuits were filed against the Morgans in the wake of the investigation.</p><p>But they continued to operate South Chicago Chapel at 2939 E. 95th St., and now dozens more families find themselves in the same position demanding answers from the Morgans and seeking accountability for their deceased loved ones. </p><p>The Morgans’ attorney declined to comment Friday and the pair did not respond to reporters outside their home.</p><div officers arrived to search the South Chicago Chapel, acting on a tip that bodies were not being stored at the proper temperature.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/07/south-side-funeral-home-bodies-families-investigation" >Families, neighbors sickened by discovery of dozens of decomposing bodies at Far South Side funeral home</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Clark Morgan led them on a walk through of the funeral home, where officers discovered 57 bodies — unrefrigerated, and in various states of decomposition, according to a police report. On Wednesday, the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation revoked Johanna Morgan's funeral director and embalmer's license. </p><p>The agency found the practice was “a danger to the public safety, interest and welfare,” and allege Johanna Morgan let “multiple decedents to be kept in an unrefrigerated area with deplorable conditions including rodent infestation, causing decomposition and maggot infestation of the bodies.”</p><p>It’s unclear why police didn’t visit the funeral home until the next day. </p><p>This was also not the first time Johanna Morgan has been fined and reprimanded by the IDFPR, according to records.</p><p>In 2024, her funeral director and embalmer license was reprimanded and she was fined $5,000 for failing to complete three records in 2020.</p><p>In 2017 her license was suspended for failure to file or pay state income taxes. She was also reprimanded and fined for failing to file a death certificate “in a timely manner.”</p><p>In April 2024, Clark Morgan was fined $10,000 and his funeral director and embalmer intern license was revoked due to “unprofessional conduct” and practicing on an expired license, according to IDFPR records. His license was suspended in 2018 due to failure to file or pay state income taxes.</p><p>The Illinois Funeral Directors Association “was horrified to learn of the events at South Side Chapel…we are angered by the indignities suffered by the decedents,” IFDA general counsel Michael Sharkey said Friday.</p><p>The IDFPR regulates funeral director and embalmers. If a funeral home sells products, such as caskets or flowers, they must obtain a business license issued by the Chicago Department of Business Affairs and Consumer Protection.</p><p>South Chicago Chapel does not have a Chicago business license, a BACP spokesperson said in an email.</p><p>In early 2025 IFDA reported the people allegedly “involved in mishandling/mistreating decedents” at Heights Crematory in Chicago Heights to the Illinois Comptroller’s Office, which oversees crematories in the state.</p><p>“It is extremely disturbing that the same individuals who appear to be involved with the events at South Side Chapel are the same persons that the Comptroller’s Office was aware of from the tragedy at Heights Crematory,” IFDA’s news release said.</p><p>“We encourage those who are seeking funeral services to look for a provider that is a member of the IFDA so that the family knows that their loved one will be treated with the respect and dignity they deserve.”</p><p>South Chicago Chapel and Heights Crematory were never members of IFDA, Sharkey said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a </div><p></p><h3><b>Tragedy in Chicago Heights </b></h3><p>The Morgans are still facing nearly two dozen of lawsuits stemming from the mishandling of remains at Chicago Heights Crematory, 230 E. 11th St.</p><p>One of the lawsuit's plaintiffs said they brought their mother’s remains to the crematory in 2020, then heard nothing from the operators for years.</p><p>It was only after they filed complaints with the Better Business Bureau and Office of the Illinois Attorney General in 2022, that the crematory provided them an urn, according to court records. </p><p>The Illinois Comptroller’s Office, which oversees crematories, opened an investigation into the business in Feb. 2025 after the IFDA received a photo of bodies being stored in trailers outside of the building. </p><p>In June 2025, that same plaintiff received a call from the controller's office informing them the remains in the urn may not be their mother's. A check of the cremation ID number confirmed they were not. </p><p>The crematory permanently ceased operation that same month. The Cook County medical examiner’s office launched a database to help people, who brought remains to Chicago Heights Crematory, recover family members.</p><p>The medical examiner's office is currently working to contact the families and loved ones of those found in South Chicago Chapel.</p><p><i>Contributing: Elijah James</i></p>
