entries.title: How Sky's Sydney Taylor and Natasha Cloud became fast friends
entries.summary: <p>In a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> season that has made everyone want to pull their hair out, two underdogs have helped redeem it: Sydney Taylor and Natasha Cloud.</p><p>Their friendship began, as many great ones do, because their lockers are next to each other’s. They got to talking about fashion first, noticing each other’s style and asking where certain pieces came from.</p><p>They share some New York-ness in their swagger. Taylor grew up on Long Island, and Cloud delighted in her stint with the Liberty last season.</p><p>Both have approached this season with a chip on their shoulder.</p><p>Cloud, 34, didn’t get picked up by the Sky until May. After the Liberty didn’t ask her back and initial offers didn’t come in, she doubted whether she would play in the WNBA at all. Taylor, 23, went undrafted and played overseas for two seasons, still believing she would make it to the league.</p><p>They’re proving the naysayers wrong. Taylor is the team’s leading scorer and a lock for the All-Rookie team. Cloud’s game shows few signs of aging, as her stat line is nearly identical to what it was last season.</p><p>Cloud said her favorite thing about Taylor’s game is the effortlessness. Her movements have the fluidity of 2025 Rookie of the Year Paige Bueckers, but she has a ‘‘Mamba’’ mentality all her own.</p><p>To show it, Cloud reenacted the three-pointer Taylor sank over A’ja Wilson in the Sky’s recent victory against the Aces.</p><p>‘‘As a rookie, for you to have that in your bag [and] to do that against the Defensive Player of the Year and eight-time All-Star, all these things?’’ Cloud said. ‘‘Cold.’’</p><p>The pair are thriving in a season of adversity. The Sky lost leading scorer Rickea Jackson four games in, and it took some wandering in the desert before they figured out how to succeed without her. Because of the hole they dug themselves, the playoffs are now a long shot.</p><p>But they’re playing good basketball now — 3-1 out of the All-Star break, with a top-five net rating in the last 15 games. Cloud calls them a sleeper team.</p><p>‘‘Whether people want to admit it or not, they don’t want to face us,’’ Cloud said.</p><p>There’s probably some truth to that. The Sky stunned the defending champion Aces and have a chance to spoil things for the Fever on Saturday at the United Center. They’ll have to do it without Taylor, who’s out with a groin injury.</p><p>After practice Friday, with Taylor lingering to shoot, Cloud reminded anyone within earshot how much Taylor loves her, pointing at their matching purple shoes for proof. There’s truth to that, too. Taylor really does look up to Cloud.</p><p>Cloud, a three-time All-Defense selection, often pulls Taylor aside with defensive pointers. She sees Taylor’s quickness and strength and coaches her on how to weaponize them.</p><p>‘‘Just giving her minute tendencies that I do that I think she can also implement into her game that create just a little bit of advantage,’’ Cloud said. ‘‘She’s such a great offensive player. I won’t allow her to box herself into one; you’re a two-way player.’’</p><p>Asked whether she has learned anything from her mentee, Cloud laughed and called out Taylor’s game-winner against the Aces. Cloud wanted to celebrate, but Taylor reminded her there were still 0.9 seconds of defense to be played.</p><p>The real answer, however, is that Taylor’s breakout has Cloud reaching deeper into her own bag. And Taylor’s feedback has given Cloud confidence as a leader.</p><p>‘‘You always think, like, ‘I hope I’m giving to the team in the best way that I can,’ ’’ Cloud said, ‘‘but you never know if that’s actually happening.’’</p><p>The Sky’s record — 12-19 — and the number of games they’ve blown mean that, come season's end, there will be plenty of soul-searching for everyone to do. But it’s not a lost season. One that has spawned the Cloud-Taylor connection can’t be.</p><p><b>NOTE:</b> Forward Azura Stevens returned to practice Friday after missing four games for personal reasons. She didn’t comment on her absence, other than to say it was “just personal stuff I was dealing with.” Coach Tyler Marsh said he expects her ramp-up to be quick.</p>

entries.title: Review: Klaus Mäkelä’s Ravinia debut delivered sublime moments, signaled commitment
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Symphony Orchestra had a big night Thursday at the Ravinia Festival as Music Director Designate Klaus Mäkelä, set to take on his full duties in September 2027, made his debut at the outdoor series in Highland Park where the ensemble has summered since 1936.</p><p>Appearances by CSO music directors at Ravinia are actually quite rare. Georg Solti and Riccardo Muti led the orchestra at other times but never while music director. And Daniel Barenboim made appearances in just two summers over his 1991-2006 tenure.</p><p>That Mäkelä, 30, would carve time out of his stuffed international schedule for a pair of concerts at Ravinia shows that he obviously wants to do things his way. It also makes evident that he is committed to this orchestra and interested in connecting with suburban audiences, who might come downtown to Orchestra Hall only sporadically or not at all.</p><p>Even better, he brought the same level of enthusiasm and intensity to this concert as does to his Orchestra Hall concerts — his purposefulness illustrated by the uncompromising black tie and white jacket he sported on this warm, steamy evening. These were all clear positives.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a60000" name="image-a60000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/19d45e4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5392x3026+0+283/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdd%2F5d%2Fed2b436a46d5a22acf3c8c2f6f40%2F2026-08-06-cso-klaus-makela-daniel-lozakovich-017.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ca9c3a3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5392x3026+0+283/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdd%2F5d%2Fed2b436a46d5a22acf3c8c2f6f40%2F2026-08-06-cso-klaus-makela-daniel-lozakovich-017.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/01228c4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5392x3026+0+283/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdd%2F5d%2Fed2b436a46d5a22acf3c8c2f6f40%2F2026-08-06-cso-klaus-makela-daniel-lozakovich-017.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Klaus Mäkelä conducts the CSO at Ravinia. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/01228c4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5392x3026+0+283/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdd%2F5d%2Fed2b436a46d5a22acf3c8c2f6f40%2F2026-08-06-cso-klaus-makela-daniel-lozakovich-017.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ee41eb3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5392x3026+0+283/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdd%2F5d%2Fed2b436a46d5a22acf3c8c2f6f40%2F2026-08-06-cso-klaus-makela-daniel-lozakovich-017.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/01228c4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5392x3026+0+283/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdd%2F5d%2Fed2b436a46d5a22acf3c8c2f6f40%2F2026-08-06-cso-klaus-makela-daniel-lozakovich-017.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The redesigned Hunter Pavilion at Ravinia Festival in Highland Park. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Ravinia Festival</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The concert was also an opportunity to take stock of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/07/10/ravinia-renovation-hunter-pavilion-cso-lizzo-acoustics-architect-history-concert-tickets" ><u>significant changes</u></a> to Ravinia’s 76-year-old main stage, now called the Hunter Pavilion, which has undergone a handsome, much-needed $70 million makeover. Improvements include a more spacious stage, a striking ziggurat-patterned acoustic shell and enhanced lighting.</p><p>But what was most important Thursday evening, of course, was the musicmaking, and Mäkelä and the orchestra delivered in convincing fashion. The unequivocal highlight of this concert came in the second half when the ensemble — augmented to 102 players (including the addition of the unusual Wagner tuba) — offered an interpretation of Richard Strauss’ “An Alpine Symphony,” Op. 64, that was nothing short of sublime.</p><p>To get a sense of the emotional impact of this performance, consider that at its deliberate, quiet conclusion, Mäkelä held his hands in front of him and froze for at least 20 seconds. And until he finally lowered his hands, there was not a hint of applause, just complete, appreciative silence — something that almost never happens, no matter how hard conductors try.</p><p>Though this 50-minute 1915 work is labeled a symphony, it is really an uninterrupted, 22-section tone poem that wordlessly tells a simple story: an ascent of an alpine peak as night turns into day and back to night, with bird calls, waterfalls and myriad other sights and sounds, all spectacularly evoked in Strauss’ magical score.</p><p>This performance throbbed with inner joy, captivating energy and masterful ease, with musicians across the orchestra making the most of their moments in the spotlight, none more memorable than a hushed, introspective solo by principal clarinetist Stephen Williamson.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-4c0000" name="image-4c0000"></a> <picture class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Klaus Mäkelä conducts with soloist Daniel Lozakovih at Ravinia.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Timothy Hiatt for the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Despite having to deal with Ravinia’s determined cicadas and other ambient outdoor sounds and the inevitable loss of aural naturalness that comes with amplification, Mäkelä and the orchestra managed to achieve an impressively refined sound, nuanced dynamics and a surprising sense of intimacy during the piece’s softest moments.</p><p>(Ravinia’s sound crew deserves considerable credit, especially the team controlling the mixing board, but also apparently contributing were the much-touted improvements to the on-stage acoustics meant to help the musicians hear each other better.)</p><p>The CSO’s superlative take on “An Alpine Symphony” more than made up for the lackluster first half, which was devoted to Jean Sibelius’ Violin Concerto in D minor, Op. 47, one of the most oft-performed works in this form.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-260000" name="module-260000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><b>Chicago Symphony Orchestra, Klaus Mäkelä, conductor</b></h3><br><b>When:</b> 7:30 p.m., Aug. 7 (Claude Debussy and Igor Stravinsky)<br><b>Where:</b> Ravinia Festival, 200 Ravinia Park Road, Highland Park<br><b>Tickets:</b> $17-$124<br><b>Info:</b> 847-266-5100; <a class="Link" href="https://www.ravinia.org/" target="_blank" >ravinia.org</a></div> </div><p>This performance just never quite gelled. It didn’t help that some of the balances were out of whack here, presumably issues with the amplification — especially the French horns being overpowering at times.</p><p>The featured soloist was 25-year-old Swedish violinist Daniel Lozakovich, clearly a favorite of Mäkelä, who brought him to Orchestra Hall for CSO concerts in 2022. He possessed the expected technical virtuosity and admirably demonstrated a feel for the turned-in, anguished sensibility of this Scandinavian music, delivering affecting turns during its meditative sections.</p><p>But during the bigger moments, his playing just wasn’t big enough. A good example came at the well-known beginning of the fast third movement with its propulsive, highly rhythmic opening motif that just needed more punch and drive than he was able to provide.</p><p>Lozakovich returned to the stage for an encore, Nathan Milstein’s “Paganiniana,” but again, there were compelling turns of phrase and moments of shining virtuosity that did not quite add up to a cohesive musical whole.</p>
